liver-b1: Hepatoma (hepatocellular carcinoma) is strongly associated with elevated AFP and may present with right upper quadrant pain. Remember: AFP elevation in an adult with a liver mass is a classic clue for HCC.
liver-b2: Focal nodular hyperplasia is a benign liver mass that is often isoechoic on ultrasound and characteristically contains a central scar. Key memory tip: “FNH = central scar” is the hallmark association.
liver-b3: The fibrous covering of the liver is called Glisson capsule. Remember: Glisson capsule surrounds the liver and also extends inward around the portal triads.
liver-b4: The middle hepatic vein is the main landmark that separates the right and left lobes of the liver sonographically. Memory aid: the middle hepatic vein runs in the main lobar fissure.
liver-b5: A TIPS creates a channel between a portal vein branch and a hepatic vein to reduce portal venous pressure. Remember: TIPS is used to treat complications of portal hypertension, such as variceal bleeding.
liver-b6: Cirrhosis is the likely diagnosis because it classically produces a coarse, heterogeneous echotexture with surface nodularity and distorted hepatic architecture. Key fact: cirrhosis often coexists with portal hypertension and increased HCC risk.
liver-b7: In a cirrhotic liver, a focal mass is most concerning for hepatoma (hepatocellular carcinoma). Remember: cirrhosis is the major predisposing condition for development of HCC.
liver-b8: The right hepatic vein divides the right lobe into anterior and posterior segments. Memory tip: right lobe segmentation follows the right hepatic vein.
liver-b9: The right intersegmental fissure contains the right hepatic vein. Remember: hepatic veins are intersegmental landmarks, while portal veins run within segments.
liver-b10: The main portal vein normally bifurcates into right and left portal vein branches. Key fact: the right portal vein then divides into anterior and posterior branches.
liver-b11: Hepatofugal flow means blood is flowing away from the liver, which is an abnormal finding commonly seen with portal hypertension. Remember: normal portal venous flow is hepatopetal—toward the liver.
liver-b12: The sampled structure is the portal vein, whose normal mean velocity is about 20 to 40 cm/sec. Memory tip: portal venous flow is normally monophasic, hepatopetal, and relatively low velocity.
liver-b13: The ligamentum teres separates the medial and lateral segments of the left lobe. Remember: in the left lobe, the ligamentum teres and ligamentum venosum are key segmental landmarks.
liver-b14: The main lobar fissure contains the middle hepatic vein, which is the principal landmark between the right and left lobes. Key fact: the gallbladder also helps identify this fissure sonographically.
liver-b15: The middle hepatic vein is not part of the porta hepatis; it courses within the liver and drains toward the IVC. Remember: the porta hepatis contains the portal vein, hepatic artery, and bile duct.
overview-b1: Twinkle artifact is a rapid color Doppler mosaic seen behind rough, highly reflective interfaces such as stones. Remember: it “sparkles” on color Doppler and can help detect calculi even when shadowing is subtle.
overview-b2: Cholecystitis commonly causes an elevated white blood cell count because it is an inflammatory/infectious process. Remember: RUQ pain plus leukocytosis is a classic clinical clue for acute cholecystitis.
overview-b3: A large acoustic interface can create repeated reflections between strong reflectors, producing false echoes. Remember: stronger interfaces increase the chance of reverberation-type artifacts.
overview-b4: Reverberation occurs when sound bounces back and forth between strong reflectors, creating multiple equally spaced echoes. Remember: the repeated lines get deeper but are not real anatomy.
overview-b5: Transitional cell carcinoma arises from urothelium, so it is common in the renal pelvis, ureter, and bladder, not the liver. Remember: think “urothelial lining” for TCC locations.
overview-b6: Ring-down artifact appears as a continuous echogenic streak distal to gas or closely spaced reflective interfaces. Remember: unlike comet-tail, ring-down is produced by resonance of trapped fluid or gas bubbles.
overview-b7: Neuroblastoma is a malignant pediatric tumor that most often arises from the adrenal gland. Remember: in children, an adrenal mass crossing the midline strongly suggests neuroblastoma.
overview-b8: A tumor marker is a biomarker produced by a cancer or by the body in response to cancer. Remember: examples include AFP and CA 19-9, which help with diagnosis or follow-up.
overview-b9: Pheochromocytoma is classically a catecholamine-secreting tumor of the adrenal gland. Remember: think adrenal mass with episodic hypertension, headaches, and palpitations.
overview-b10: A lesion with echotexture similar to normal liver is isoechoic. Remember: isoechoic masses can be harder to see, so contour bulge or vessel displacement may be the only clue.
overview-b11: Mirror image artifact occurs when sound reflects off a strong specular reflector and duplicates a structure on the opposite side. Remember: the diaphragm commonly creates mirror image of liver or vessels.
overview-b12: The pancreas is primarily a retroperitoneal organ, so it is not considered intraperitoneal. Remember: liver, gallbladder, and spleen are intraperitoneal, but pancreas sits posteriorly.
overview-b13: Increasing PRF helps correct aliasing by raising the Nyquist limit in Doppler imaging. Remember: aliasing happens when blood velocity exceeds half the PRF.
overview-b14: The ovaries are pelvic intraperitoneal structures, not retroperitoneal organs. Remember: kidneys, adrenal glands, and many abdominal lymph nodes lie in the retroperitoneum.
overview-b15: Morison pouch is the posterior right subhepatic space between the liver and right kidney. Remember: it is a key FAST exam site because free fluid often collects there first in a supine patient.
overview-b31: This artifact is caused by side/grating lobes—non-perpendicular peripheral beams outside the main beam that strike a reflector and place echoes in the wrong location. Remember: energy off the main axis can create false internal echoes.
overview-b32: Aliasing occurs in Doppler when blood velocity exceeds the Nyquist limit, causing color or spectral wraparound. Remember: increasing PRF/scale or lowering the transmitted frequency can reduce aliasing.
overview-b33: The liver is considered intraperitoneal because it is invested by peritoneum except at bare areas. Remember: kidneys, aorta, and IVC are primarily retroperitoneal structures.
overview-b34: A yolk sac tumor is a malignant germ cell tumor of the testis, especially important in pediatric patients. Remember: it is the most common testicular tumor in young boys.
overview-b35: Refraction is the bending of the sound beam at an interface when propagation speeds differ and the beam hits at an oblique angle. Remember: oblique incidence plus different sound speeds causes beam misregistration.
overview-b36: Paracolic gutters are the peritoneal spaces that run along the ascending and descending colon. Remember: fluid can track through these gutters to spread within the abdomen.
overview-b37: Angiomyolipoma is a common benign renal tumor made of blood vessels, smooth muscle, and fat. Remember: the fat content often makes it appear markedly echogenic on ultrasound.
overview-b38: The thyroid gland is an endocrine gland, not a salivary gland. Remember: the major salivary glands are parotid, submandibular, and sublingual.
overview-b39: Pheochromocytoma is not typically classified as a pediatric malignant tumor in this group, unlike hepatoblastoma, neuroblastoma, and nephroblastoma. Remember: the classic pediatric malignancies here are liver, adrenal/sympathetic, and Wilms tumors.
overview-b40: A teratoma contains tissues derived from all three germ cell layers: ectoderm, mesoderm, and endoderm. Remember: teratomas may contain mixed elements like hair, teeth, or cartilage.
overview-b41: Elevated WBC is a sign because it is an objective, measurable finding observed by the clinician or lab. Remember: signs are objective; symptoms like pain, nausea, and headache are subjective.
overview-b42: Hematocrit is most helpful after recent trauma because it helps assess blood loss and possible hemorrhage. Remember: falling hematocrit can indicate ongoing internal bleeding.
overview-b43: An insulinoma is a usually benign pancreatic islet cell tumor that secretes insulin. Remember: excess insulin causes hypoglycemia, a classic clinical clue.
overview-b44: A granuloma is a masslike collection of inflammatory cells, often formed in chronic inflammation. Remember: granulomas are classically associated with infections like TB or inflammatory conditions such as sarcoidosis.
overview-b45: A hematoma is a localized collection of blood, usually due to trauma or bleeding. Remember: on ultrasound, its appearance changes over time as the blood ages.
overview-b46: Beta-hCG is a recognized tumor marker for certain testicular malignancies, especially nonseminomatous germ cell tumors. Remember: testicular cancer markers commonly tested are beta-hCG, AFP, and LDH.
overview-b47: Choriocarcinoma is composed of trophoblastic cells, the same cell type involved in placental tissue. A helpful clue is that these tumors often produce beta-hCG.
overview-b48: Gallstones strongly attenuate sound, producing clean posterior acoustic shadowing. Remember: stones, bone, and calcifications are classic causes of shadowing on ultrasound.
overview-b49: Exudate ascites is associated with malignancy, infection, or inflammation because it contains more protein and cellular material. Think: cancer-related ascites is usually exudative, not transudative.
overview-b50: Twinkle artifact appears on color Doppler behind rough, highly reflective surfaces such as calculi and calcifications. Remember: a kidney stone may 'twinkle' even when shadowing is subtle.
overview-b51: The pancreas has both exocrine function (digestive enzyme secretion) and endocrine function (insulin and glucagon production). Memory tip: acinar cells are exocrine, islet cells are endocrine.
overview-b52: Cirrhosis commonly causes portal hypertension and low albumin states, both of which promote ascites formation. Remember: cirrhosis is one of the classic abdominal causes of free fluid.
overview-b53: Elastography evaluates tissue stiffness, helping differentiate softer from firmer tissue. Key fact: malignant tissue is often stiffer than benign tissue, which is why elastography can be useful.
overview-b54: Harmonic imaging uses nonlinear propagation of ultrasound through tissue to generate harmonic frequencies, improving image quality and resolution. Remember: tissue harmonics reduce clutter and sharpen borders.
overview-b55: A mural nodule means there is a solid component along the cyst wall, so the lesion is no longer a simple cyst. Simple cysts should be anechoic, thin-walled, and without internal solid elements.
overview-b56: Creatinine rises when renal filtration is impaired, so an elevated level suggests renal disease or dysfunction. Remember: creatinine is a key lab marker of kidney function.
overview-b57: The space of Retzius is another name for the retropubic space, located between the pubic symphysis and urinary bladder. Memory aid: 'Retzius' = 'retro' pubic.
overview-b58: MRI does not use ionizing radiation, X-rays, or radionuclides; it uses magnetic fields and radiofrequency pulses. Remember: radiography, CT, and nuclear medicine all involve radiation, but MRI does not.
overview-b59: Urinary tract infections are among the most common hospital-acquired infections, often related to catheter use. Key fact: indwelling urinary catheters greatly increase nosocomial UTI risk.
overview-b60: von Hippel-Lindau disease is a rare inherited disorder that causes cysts and tumors in multiple organs. Remember: it is classically associated with renal cysts/carcinoma and pheochromocytoma.
overview-b16: Hypernephroma is an older term for renal cell carcinoma, the most common primary malignant renal tumor in adults. Remember: hypernephroma = RCC, not Wilms tumor, which is nephroblastoma.
overview-b17: Comet-tail artifact is produced by multiple closely spaced reflective interfaces, such as tiny gas bubbles, creating a tapering series of echoes. Key memory aid: gas commonly causes bright comet-tail reverberations.
overview-b18: Cholangiocarcinoma is carcinoma arising from the bile ducts. Recall: 'cholangio-' refers to bile vessels/ducts, whereas hepatocellular carcinoma arises from liver cells.
overview-b19: A side lobe artifact occurs when off-axis sound beams place echoes in the main beam path, creating false internal echoes. Remember: side lobes often make a simple cyst appear to contain debris.
overview-b20: Aliasing occurs when the pulse repetition frequency is too low to accurately sample the Doppler shift, causing wraparound of the signal. Key fact: aliasing happens when Doppler shift exceeds the Nyquist limit.
overview-b21: Hepatoma refers to a malignant tumor of the liver, commonly synonymous with hepatocellular carcinoma. Remember: 'hepato-' means liver, and hepatoma is not a benign lesion.
overview-b22: Comet-tail artifact is a short, closely spaced reverberation that tapers posteriorly from a highly reflective interface. A good clue is its bright triangular tail, often seen with metal, cholesterol crystals, or gas.
overview-b23: Hepatoblastoma is a malignant liver tumor seen primarily in children. Memory tip: 'blastoma' often indicates an embryonal or pediatric malignancy.
overview-b24: The lesser sac, or omental bursa, is the peritoneal space located between the stomach and pancreas. Remember: fluid in the lesser sac can collect just posterior to the stomach.
overview-b25: Wilms tumor is another name for nephroblastoma, a pediatric renal malignancy. Key fact: Wilms = nephroblastoma, while neuroblastoma usually arises from the adrenal region.
overview-b26: Angiosarcoma is a malignant vascular tumor and is classically associated with the spleen in abdominal imaging. Remember: 'angio-' means vessel, so think of highly vascular organs like the spleen.
overview-b27: Refraction artifact occurs when the sound beam bends at tissue boundaries, causing structures to be misplaced or duplicated. A classic setup is scanning through the rectus muscle in the midline, which can refract the beam.
overview-b28: The spleen is not an endocrine organ; it is primarily a lymphatic and hematologic organ. Remember: thyroid, thymus, and pancreas all have endocrine function, but the spleen does not secrete hormones.
overview-b29: Anisotropy changes tendon echogenicity when the beam is not perpendicular, making the tendon appear falsely hypoechoic. Key fact: tendons are angle-dependent, so a small probe tilt can dramatically change their brightness.
overview-b30: A gastrinoma is most commonly found in the pancreas and is one of the pancreatic islet cell tumors. Remember: despite the name, gastrin-secreting tumors are usually in the 'gastrinoma triangle,' often involving the pancreas.
liver-b31: The inferior extension of the caudate lobe is the papillary process, a normal anatomic variant that projects anteriorly. Remember: papillary process belongs to the caudate lobe, whereas Riedel’s lobe is an inferior tongue-like extension of the right lobe.
liver-b32: With splenomegaly and hepatofugal portal flow, the image most likely shows esophageal varices from portal hypertension. Key fact: left gastric (coronary) vein enlargement commonly feeds esophageal varices in cirrhosis.
liver-b33: Figure 2-60 suggests cirrhosis with portal hypertension, and a shrunken right lobe is a classic associated sonographic finding. Memory aid: cirrhosis often causes a small nodular liver, especially right lobe atrophy with relative caudate enlargement.
liver-b34: Narrowing of the hepatic veins is least likely because the case points to cirrhosis/portal hypertension, not hepatic venous outflow obstruction. Remember: hepatic vein narrowing is more characteristic of Budd-Chiari syndrome.
liver-b35: Hepatitis C has historically been the most common indication for liver transplantation because chronic infection often progresses to cirrhosis and liver failure. Key fact: transplant questions commonly link Hep C with end-stage liver disease.
liver-b36: Fatty infiltration commonly produces elevated liver function tests, even when symptoms are minimal. Remember: fatty liver is often clinically silent but biochemically abnormal before major symptoms appear.
liver-b37: After birth, the ductus venosus closes and becomes the ligamentum venosum. Memory tip: the umbilical vein becomes the ligamentum teres, while the ductus venosus becomes the ligamentum venosum.
liver-b38: A diffusely echogenic liver that is difficult to penetrate is classic for fatty liver disease due to increased attenuation. Key fact: steatosis makes the liver bright and obscures deeper structures like the diaphragm.
liver-b39: Alcoholism is the most common cause of cirrhosis in classic sonography teaching. Remember: chronic alcohol injury leads to fibrosis, nodularity, and portal hypertension.
liver-b40: Pericholecystic fluid is not a typical clinical finding of hepatitis; jaundice, fever, and chills may occur. Key fact: pericholecystic fluid suggests gallbladder pathology such as cholecystitis rather than primary hepatitis.
liver-b41: Immunocompromised patients are especially prone to hepatic candidiasis, a fungal infection often seen with multiple tiny lesions. Memory aid: think 'candida in compromised hosts,' especially in neutropenic patients.
liver-b42: Hepatic artery contraction is not a recognized sequela of cirrhosis, whereas portal hypertension, splenomegaly, and even portal vein thrombosis can occur. Remember: cirrhosis increases resistance to portal flow rather than causing hepatic arterial contraction.
liver-b43: Normal portal venous flow toward the liver is called hepatopetal. Easy memory trick: 'petal' points to the liver, while 'fugal' means fleeing away from it.
liver-b44: A hyperechoic mass with a hypoechoic halo is worrisome because the halo is a classic malignant feature. Key fact: a 'target' or halo appearance in the liver raises concern for metastasis or hepatocellular carcinoma.
liver-b45: Hepatic adenomas can undergo malignant degeneration, which makes them clinically important despite being benign tumors. Remember: adenomas are classically linked to oral contraceptive use and carry a risk of hemorrhage too.
liver-b16: Right-sided heart failure causes elevated central venous pressure, leading to passive congestion and dilation of the IVC and hepatic veins. Remember: hepatic veins drain directly into the IVC, so they enlarge together in right heart failure.
liver-b17: A cavernous hemangioma is the most common benign liver tumor and is often found incidentally in young, asymptomatic women. Key memory fact: hemangiomas are classically well-defined and usually hyperechoic on ultrasound.
liver-b18: Amebic liver abscess is linked to Entamoeba histolytica infection, commonly acquired from contaminated food or water in endemic regions. Remember: travel to developing areas plus contaminated water should suggest amebic abscess.
liver-b19: The right portal vein normally divides into anterior and posterior branches to supply the right hepatic lobe. Memory tip: right lobe segmentation follows anterior/posterior, while the left lobe is medial/lateral.
liver-b20: A normal main portal vein diameter should not exceed 13 mm in adults. Remember the cutoff: 'portal vein = 13' is a classic sonography measurement associated with possible portal hypertension when enlarged.
liver-b21: The right lobe is divided into anterior and posterior segments in standard hepatic anatomy. Helpful memory fact: right = anterior/posterior, left = medial/lateral.
liver-b22: Portal veins have echogenic, brighter walls because they are surrounded by fibrous tissue, unlike hepatic veins. Remember: bright walls point to portal veins, while hepatic veins have less conspicuous walls.
liver-b23: The left lobe is divided into medial and lateral segments in liver anatomy. Memory aid: left = medial/lateral, contrasting with the right lobe’s anterior/posterior division.
liver-b24: The normal hepatic artery shows a low-resistance waveform because the liver has continuous metabolic demand, so forward diastolic flow remains present. Remember: brisk systolic upstroke plus persistent diastolic flow indicates low resistance.
liver-b25: Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease commonly includes multiple hepatic cysts, so liver cysts with this clinical pattern strongly suggest ADPKD. Key fact: the liver is the most common extra-renal site of cyst formation in ADPKD.
liver-b26: Budd–Chiari syndrome is hepatic venous outflow obstruction, so the hepatic veins become narrowed or difficult to visualize. Remember: Budd–Chiari primarily affects hepatic veins, not the portal vein or bile ducts.
liver-b27: A Riedel lobe is a normal variant consisting of a tongue-like inferior projection of the right hepatic lobe. Memory fact: it can mimic hepatomegaly or a mass if you do not recognize the variant.
liver-b28: The left portal vein divides into medial and lateral branches to supply the left hepatic lobe. Remember: left lobe segmentation is medial/lateral, opposite the right lobe’s anterior/posterior branching.
liver-b29: After birth, the left umbilical vein fibroses and becomes the ligamentum teres. Memory tip: ligamentum teres lies in the falciform ligament and is a key landmark in the left lobe.
liver-b30: Normal hepatic vein flow is triphasic because it reflects pressure changes from the right atrium during the cardiac cycle. Remember: hepatic veins are the liver vessels most influenced by cardiac pulsatility.
liver-b46: Metastatic liver disease is the most common liver malignancy because the liver frequently filters tumor cells from other primary cancers, especially colon, lung, and breast. Remember: primary liver cancers are less common than secondary spread.
liver-b47: Hepatic adenoma is strongly linked to oral contraceptive use due to estrogen stimulation of hepatocytes. Key memory fact: adenomas have a risk of hemorrhage, especially in young women on OCPs.
liver-b48: Hemangioendothelioma is the most common benign hepatic tumor of infancy and childhood. Remember: it is a vascular lesion, so think pediatric liver mass with possible high-flow vascular features.
liver-b49: Reduction in AFP is the exception because hepatocellular carcinoma more commonly causes elevated alpha-fetoprotein levels, not decreased levels. Memory tip: HCC and high AFP are a classic association.
liver-b50: Beckwith–Wiedemann syndrome is associated with an increased risk of hepatoblastoma, a primary malignant liver tumor in children. Remember: pediatric overgrowth syndromes raise concern for embryonal tumors.
liver-b51: Echinococcus granulosus causes hydatid disease, producing hydatid liver cysts. Key fact: these cysts may show daughter cysts, a classic imaging clue for echinococcal infection.
liver-b52: Cirrhosis most likely causes decreased albumin because chronic liver damage impairs the liver’s protein-synthesizing function. Remember: albumin reflects hepatic synthetic ability, which falls in advanced chronic liver disease.
liver-b53: Kupffer cells are the liver’s resident macrophages that engulf pathogens, debris, and damaged cells. Memory fact: they line the hepatic sinusoids and serve as the liver’s main phagocytic defense.
liver-b54: Periportal cuffing is associated with hepatitis because inflammation around the portal triads increases periportal echogenicity. Remember: periportal edema or inflammation often points to acute hepatic inflammatory disease.
liver-b55: Hemochromatosis is the inherited disorder causing excessive absorption of dietary iron with iron deposition in organs including the liver. Memory tip: think bronze diabetes and iron overload.
liver-b56: Von Hippel–Lindau disease is linked to cyst formation in multiple organs, including the liver. Remember: VHL is a multisystem inherited disorder known for cysts and vascular tumors.
liver-b57: Wilson disease can appear sonographically similar to hepatitis because both may produce diffuse hepatic parenchymal changes. Key fact: Wilson disease is a copper storage disorder, especially affecting the liver and brain.
liver-b58: Cavernous transformation of the portal vein develops in chronic portal vein thrombosis as collateral veins form around the occluded vessel. Remember: it is a collateral bypass pattern, not normal portal flow.
liver-b59: Pyogenic hepatic abscess can follow intra-abdominal infections such as appendicitis, diverticulitis, or cholecystitis through portal venous spread. Memory fact: pyogenic abscesses are bacterial and often arise from nearby infection.
liver-b60: Hepatoblastoma is the most likely diagnosis in a 5-year-old with abdominal enlargement because it is the most common primary malignant liver tumor in young children. Remember: hepatoblastoma is a classic pediatric liver malignancy.
gallbladder-b16: Hartmann pouch is a saclike outpouching of the gallbladder neck, often where stones may lodge. Remember: Hartmann pouch sits near the cystic duct, so think “neck region.”
gallbladder-b17: The gallbladder drains into and communicates with the biliary tree through the cystic duct. Key memory fact: cystic duct + common hepatic duct join to form the common bile duct.
gallbladder-b18: The junctional fold is a normal fold located at the gallbladder neck. Remember it as the fold at the “junction” between the neck and body.
gallbladder-b19: Empyema means the gallbladder lumen is filled with pus, usually from severe infection. Memory tip: “empyema” anywhere in the body refers to purulent material in a cavity.
gallbladder-b20: Cholelithiasis simply means gallstones within the gallbladder or biliary system. Break it down: “chole” = bile, “lith” = stone.
gallbladder-b21: Strawberry gallbladder is the classic gross appearance of cholesterolosis, caused by cholesterol deposition in the gallbladder wall. Remember: tiny yellow cholesterol flecks create the strawberry-like pattern.
gallbladder-b22: A Phrygian cap is the most common normal variant in gallbladder shape, produced by folding of the fundus. Memory fact: it is a congenital fold, not a pathologic lesion.
gallbladder-b23: Normal gallbladder transverse diameter should not exceed about 5 cm. A larger diameter suggests distention, often from fasting or obstruction.
gallbladder-b24: If acute cholecystitis perforates, bile and infection can spill into the abdomen and cause peritonitis. Remember: rupture of an inflamed gallbladder is dangerous because peritonitis can be life-threatening.
gallbladder-b25: Gallbladder polyps are focal intraluminal lesions, not a typical cause of diffuse wall thickening. In contrast, inflammation and systemic diseases commonly thicken the wall diffusely.
gallbladder-b26: This statement is false because women, not men, are more likely to develop cholelithiasis. Memory aid: the classic risk profile is the “4 Fs” — female, forty, fertile, fat.
gallbladder-b27: WES sign stands for Wall-Echo-Shadow and indicates a gallbladder packed with stones. Remember the sequence: anterior wall, bright stone echo, then clean posterior acoustic shadowing.
gallbladder-b28: Adenomyomatosis is most often an incidental finding and patients are usually asymptomatic. Key fact: it commonly shows comet-tail artifacts from Rokitansky-Aschoff sinuses.
gallbladder-b29: Tumefactive sludge can mimic gallbladder carcinoma because it may appear masslike without strong shadowing. A helpful clue is that sludge often layers or moves with changes in patient position.
gallbladder-b30: The champagne sign is associated with emphysematous cholecystitis due to gas in the gallbladder lumen or wall. Memory tip: gas creates bright, bubbly echoes—like champagne bubbles.
gallbladder-b1: Hepatization of the gallbladder describes sludge filling the lumen so completely that it appears solid and liver-like on ultrasound. Remember: dense sludge can make the gallbladder mimic hepatic echotexture.
gallbladder-b2: Adenomyomatosis is classically identified by gallbladder wall thickening with Rokitansky-Aschoff sinuses, often producing comet-tail artifact. Memory aid: comet-tail in the gallbladder wall strongly suggests adenomyomatosis.
gallbladder-b3: Painless jaundice with a palpable enlarged gallbladder is the classic Courvoisier sign, often linked to malignant biliary obstruction rather than stones. Remember: 'palpable + painless' points to Courvoisier gallbladder.
gallbladder-b4: The mucosal layer is the innermost lining of the gallbladder wall. Think of the wall layers from inside out: mucosal, fibromuscular, then serosal.
gallbladder-b5: Alpha-fetoprotein is primarily a tumor marker, especially for hepatocellular carcinoma, not a routine lab for suspected gallbladder disease. In contrast, ALP, ALT, and bilirubin help assess biliary obstruction or inflammation.
gallbladder-b6: A positive Murphy sign and elevated WBC strongly support acute cholecystitis, especially when correlated with typical sonographic findings. Key fact: acute inflammation commonly presents with pain, leukocytosis, and sonographic Murphy sign.
gallbladder-b7: The cystic artery most commonly arises from the right hepatic artery within the hepatobiliary triangle. Memory tip: right hepatic gives off the vessel that feeds the right-sided gallbladder.
gallbladder-b8: The fibromuscular layer is the middle layer of the gallbladder wall. Remember the sequence: mucosal inner layer, fibromuscular middle layer, serosal outer layer.
gallbladder-b9: The main lobar fissure is a reliable sonographic landmark because it leads from the right portal vein region toward the gallbladder neck. Memory aid: follow the MLF to find the gallbladder.
gallbladder-b10: Ascites typically causes diffuse, not focal, gallbladder wall thickening. Focal thickening is more associated with intrinsic gallbladder abnormalities like polyps, adenomyomatosis, or an adhered stone.
gallbladder-b11: Cholecystokinin stimulates gallbladder contraction after a fatty meal to release bile into the duodenum. Remember: CCK = contracts the gallbladder.
gallbladder-b12: A normal gallbladder wall should measure 3 mm or less when the patient is fasting. Key fact: wall thickening beyond 3 mm raises concern for inflammation or systemic disease.
gallbladder-b13: Sickle cell disease predisposes to pigment stone formation from chronic hemolysis and is more prevalent in people of African descent. Memory tip: hemolysis increases bilirubin, which promotes pigment gallstones.
gallbladder-b14: The direct arterial supply to the gallbladder is the cystic artery. Remember: cystic artery specifically serves the gallbladder, while the right hepatic artery is its usual parent vessel.
gallbladder-b15: The serosal layer is the outermost covering of the gallbladder wall. Think inside out: mucosal, fibromuscular, serosal.
gallbladder-b31: Gallbladder perforation is the complication of acute cholecystitis in which the inflamed wall tears. Remember: perforation = rupture of the wall, often with adjacent fluid or abscess formation.
gallbladder-b32: Adenomyomatosis causes focal wall thickening with comet-tail artifact from cholesterol crystals in Rokitansky–Aschoff sinuses. Key memory aid: comet-tail plus wall thickening strongly suggests adenomyomatosis.
gallbladder-b33: Acalculous cholecystitis occurs without gallstones, so cholelithiasis would not be expected. Remember: 'acalculous' literally means absence of calculi, though wall thickening, fluid, and Murphy sign may still occur.
gallbladder-b34: Chronic cholecystitis commonly results from repeated or intermittent cystic duct obstruction by gallstones. Memory tip: chronic disease develops from recurrent attacks rather than a single acute obstruction.
gallbladder-b35: A Phrygian cap is just a normal gallbladder variant, not a predisposition to stones. Remember: pregnancy, oral contraceptives, and TPN all promote bile stasis or composition changes that increase stone risk.
gallbladder-b36: A gallbladder polyp is typically nonmobile and nonshadowing because it is attached to the wall. Key fact: stones usually shadow and move, while polyps stay fixed.
gallbladder-b37: Murphy sign is focal tenderness over the gallbladder when pressure is applied with the probe. Remember: sonographic Murphy sign helps support acute cholecystitis when the patient hurts exactly at the gallbladder.
gallbladder-b38: Emphysematous cholecystitis is more likely in diabetic patients because gas-forming organisms infect the gallbladder wall or lumen. Memory aid: diabetes plus acute cholecystitis should raise concern for intraluminal or intramural gas.
gallbladder-b39: Adenomyomatosis features cholesterol crystals within Rokitansky–Aschoff sinuses, producing classic comet-tail artifact. Remember: RA sinuses are the hallmark structural change in adenomyomatosis.
gallbladder-b40: The spiral valves of Heister are folds located in the cystic duct. Key fact: they can make catheter passage difficult and help identify the cystic duct anatomically.
gallbladder-b41: A bilobed gallbladder can appear hourglass-shaped because it is divided into two connected chambers. Memory tip: 'bi-lobed' means two lobes, creating the constricted middle appearance.
gallbladder-b42: A Courvoisier gallbladder is a distended, palpable gallbladder classically associated with malignant distal biliary obstruction, especially a pancreatic head mass. Remember: painless jaundice plus enlarged gallbladder suggests pancreatic head cancer.
gallbladder-b43: Porcelain gallbladder refers to calcification of the gallbladder wall. Key memory aid: 'porcelain' describes the brittle, calcified shell-like appearance of the wall.
gallbladder-b44: The duodenum produces cholecystokinin, which stimulates gallbladder contraction after a fatty meal. Remember: CCK comes from the small bowel, not the gallbladder itself.
gallbladder-b45: Adenomyomatosis classically produces comet-tail artifact from cholesterol crystals trapped in Rokitansky–Aschoff sinuses. Memory aid: comet-tail in the gallbladder wall points to adenomyomatosis.
gallbladder-b46: Kawasaki disease is a vasculitis that can involve the gallbladder and cause hydrops, especially in children. Remember: Kawasaki affects medium-sized arteries, and gallbladder hydrops is a recognized abdominal manifestation.
gallbladder-b47: Unconjugated bilirubin is also called indirect bilirubin because it has not yet been processed by the liver. Memory tip: indirect = not yet direct to the bile ducts.
gallbladder-b48: Murphy sign may be absent in emphysematous cholecystitis, even though diabetes, fever, and gas in the gallbladder wall are classic findings. Remember: this severe infection can present atypically, especially in diabetic patients.
gallbladder-b49: Xanthogranulomatous cholecystitis is a rare chronic inflammatory gallbladder disease with intramural accumulation of inflammatory cells. Key clue: the name 'xantho' suggests lipid-laden macrophages within the wall.
gallbladder-b50: Biliary obstruction from gallstones commonly raises direct (conjugated) bilirubin because conjugated bile cannot drain normally. Remember: obstructive jaundice = elevated direct bilirubin.
gallbladder-b51: Porcelain gallbladder is calcification of the gallbladder wall and is often found incidentally in asymptomatic patients. Memory tip: 'porcelain' describes the brittle, calcified wall appearance.
gallbladder-b52: Gangrenous cholecystitis causes ischemia and wall necrosis, leading to irregular wall bulges, sloughed membranes, and ulcerative craters. Remember: gangrene means devitalized tissue, so the wall looks disrupted rather than just inflamed.
gallbladder-b53: Chronic cholecystitis increases the likelihood of gallbladder carcinoma because long-standing inflammation predisposes to malignant change. Key fact: chronic irritation is a classic cancer risk factor in the gallbladder.
gallbladder-b54: Gallbladder polyps larger than 1 cm are more suspicious for carcinoma and often warrant closer evaluation. Remember: 10 mm is the common malignancy concern threshold for gallbladder polyps.
gallbladder-b55: A floating gallbladder is more prone to torsion because excessive mobility allows it to twist on its mesentery. Memory aid: no firm attachment means greater chance of rotation.
gallbladder-b56: Gallbladder polyps, especially cholesterol polyps, result from cholesterol and triglyceride accumulation in the gallbladder wall. Remember: cholesterol polyps are the most common benign gallbladder polyp.
gallbladder-b57: The gallbladder is divided into the fundus, body, and neck; it does not have a 'head.' Memory tip: 'head' is a pancreatic term, not a gallbladder section.
gallbladder-b58: Empyema of the gallbladder is also called suppurative cholecystitis because the lumen fills with pus. Remember: suppurative literally means pus-forming infection.
gallbladder-b59: A gallstone impacted in the cystic duct can obstruct outflow and lead to a hydropic gallbladder. Key fact: hydrops means distention of the gallbladder with clear mucoid fluid after prolonged obstruction.
gallbladder-b60: Weight gain is not typically associated with gallbladder carcinoma; patients more often have jaundice, hepatomegaly, and elevated ALP. Remember: malignancy usually causes weight loss, not weight gain.
biliary-b1: Biliary atresia is a congenital narrowing or obliteration of the bile ducts, presenting with persistent neonatal jaundice. Remember: look for the triangular cord sign and a small or absent gallbladder.
biliary-b2: Ascariasis is caused by Ascaris lumbricoides, a parasitic roundworm that can migrate into the biliary system. Remember: biliary ascariasis may appear as long echogenic tubular structures within ducts.
biliary-b3: Cholangiocarcinoma is the primary malignancy arising from the biliary epithelium. Remember: “cholangio-” refers to bile ducts, so cholangiocarcinoma means bile duct cancer.
biliary-b4: Charcot triad—fever, jaundice, and right upper quadrant pain—is the classic presentation of cholangitis. Remember: this triad is a hallmark clue for ascending biliary infection.
biliary-b5: The ampulla of Vater is the short common channel where the common bile duct and pancreatic duct join before entering the duodenum. Remember: this junction empties at the major duodenal papilla.
biliary-b6: Creatinine mainly reflects renal function, so it is the least helpful for suspected biliary tract disease. Remember: biliary evaluation relies more on cholestatic and hepatic markers like ALP, GGT, and ALT.
biliary-b7: Choledocholithiasis means a stone within the common bile duct or biliary tree. Remember: “choledocho-” refers to the common bile duct and “-lithiasis” means stones.
biliary-b8: The triangular cord sign is a classic sonographic finding associated with biliary atresia. Remember: it represents echogenic fibrous tissue anterior to the portal vein in infants with extrahepatic obstruction.
biliary-b9: Jaundice is the yellow discoloration of the skin and sclera caused by elevated bilirubin from liver disease or biliary obstruction. Remember: scleral icterus is often one of the earliest visible signs.
biliary-b10: A Klatskin tumor is a hilar cholangiocarcinoma located at the junction of the right and left hepatic ducts. Remember: “hilar” bile duct tumors commonly cause intrahepatic ductal dilatation.
biliary-b11: Cholangitis means inflammation, usually infection, of the bile ducts. Remember: the suffix “-itis” means inflammation, so cholangitis literally means inflamed bile ducts.
biliary-b12: Mirizzi syndrome results from an impacted stone in the cystic duct or gallbladder neck causing obstructive jaundice, pain, and fever. Remember: it produces extrinsic compression of the common hepatic duct.
biliary-b13: Pneumobilia means air within the biliary tree. Remember: on ultrasound, air causes bright echoes with dirty shadowing or ring-down artifact in the bile ducts.
biliary-b14: Caroli disease is associated with the central dot sign, seen as an echogenic dot within a dilated duct from fibrovascular bundles. Remember: this finding helps distinguish saccular intrahepatic duct dilatation.
biliary-b15: The spiral valves of Heister are mucosal folds located in the cystic duct. Remember: they help keep the cystic duct patent and can make catheterization or stone passage more difficult.
biliary-b31: A Klatskin tumor is a hilar cholangiocarcinoma arising at the junction of the right and left hepatic ducts. Remember: “Klatskin = confluence cancer” of the proximal biliary tree.
biliary-b32: The bile duct wall should not exceed 5 mm in thickness; a thicker wall suggests inflammation or other pathology. Memory tip: ducts are normally thin-walled, so “5 mm is the upper wall limit.”
biliary-b33: Choledocholithiasis commonly causes obstructive findings like jaundice, elevated bilirubin, and elevated ALP, but not elevated BUN. BUN reflects renal function or dehydration, not biliary obstruction.
biliary-b34: With biliary obstruction, the extrahepatic ducts usually dilate before the intrahepatic ducts become enlarged. Think: the blockage effect appears first closest to the main outflow pathway.
biliary-b35: Choledochal cysts are typically congenital and far more plausible in pediatric patients than as a common adult cause of CBD obstruction. In adults, stones, pancreatitis, and pancreatic carcinoma are much more typical.
biliary-b36: Acute bacterial, AIDS-related, and oriental cholangitis are recognized forms, but “parabolic” cholangitis is not a real entity. Easy memory aid: if it sounds geometric, it is probably not pathology.
biliary-b37: Bilirubin is the yellow bile pigment formed from hemoglobin breakdown of aging red blood cells. Remember: biliverdin is green, bilirubin is the yellow pigment linked with jaundice.
biliary-b38: A choledochal cyst is a congenital cystic dilation of the common bile duct, classically seen in pediatric patients. Key fact: this condition increases the risk of cholangitis and later malignancy.
biliary-b39: A common bile duct up to 1 cm can be considered normal in older patients or after cholecystectomy. Memory tip: the CBD may enlarge slightly with age or after gallbladder removal.
biliary-b40: Choledocholithiasis is the most common cause of obstructive jaundice because stones in the common bile duct physically block bile flow. Think: stones are far more common than tumors or congenital causes.
biliary-b41: Pneumobilia is most likely after recent biliary surgery because air can enter the biliary tree during intervention. On ultrasound, remember that air produces bright echoes with dirty shadowing or ring-down artifact.
biliary-b42: The pseudogallbladder sign is associated with biliary atresia, where a small fluid-filled structure mimics a gallbladder. Key memory fact: biliary atresia often presents in jaundiced infants with absent or abnormal extrahepatic ducts.
biliary-b43: Triangular cord sign is a sonographic sign of biliary atresia, so it would be least likely if the figure shows a different biliary disorder. Jaundice and elevated bilirubin/ALP are common in many obstructive biliary conditions.
biliary-b44: The arrow indicates the hepatic artery, an important landmark in the porta hepatis adjacent to the bile ducts and portal vein. Remember the portal triad: portal vein, hepatic artery, and bile duct.
biliary-b45: Cholangitis is infection/inflammation of the bile ducts and may show ductal wall thickening and hyperemia near the hepatic artery region. Key fact: it often presents with Charcot triad—fever, jaundice, and RUQ pain.
biliary-b16: Sclerosing cholangitis causes inflammatory fibrosis and thickening of the bile ducts, classically affecting young men and strongly associated with ulcerative colitis/IBD. Remember: PSC = "beaded" ducts on imaging and bowel disease association.
biliary-b17: A distal common hepatic duct obstruction blocks bile flow coming from the liver, so the ducts upstream of the blockage—the intrahepatic ducts—dilate. Key rule: structures proximal to an obstruction enlarge, distal segments usually do not.
biliary-b18: The intrahepatic radicles are the smallest, earliest collecting ducts within the liver, making them the most proximal part of the biliary tree. Think: bile starts in the liver and then flows outward to larger extrahepatic ducts.
biliary-b19: Pneumobilia means air in the biliary tree, and air characteristically produces ring-down artifact on ultrasound. Memory tip: gas creates dirty echoes/artifacts, not clean fluid enhancement.
biliary-b20: The common bile duct is the most distal major portion of the biliary tree because it carries bile toward the ampulla and duodenum. Remember the flow sequence: intrahepatic ducts → hepatic ducts → common bile duct.
biliary-b21: ERCP is an invasive procedure that cannulates the biliary system, so it can introduce bacteria and lead to cholangitis. Key fact: instrumentation of an obstructed biliary tree increases infection risk.
biliary-b22: A distal common duct obstruction causes backup throughout the entire biliary system, so the CBD, gallbladder, common hepatic duct, and intrahepatic ducts may all dilate. Remember: the farther distal the blockage, the more proximal structures are affected.
biliary-b23: The sphincter of Oddi is the muscular valve that regulates bile and pancreatic juice flow into the duodenum. Memory aid: it sits at the distal biliary-pancreatic outlet near the ampulla.
biliary-b24: The distal common bile duct is the most common site of biliary obstruction because stones frequently lodge near the pancreatic head/ampullary region. Remember: distal obstructions often produce more extensive upstream ductal dilatation.
biliary-b25: Cholangitis is infection/inflammation of the bile ducts and commonly presents with fever, leukocytosis, RUQ pain, ductal dilatation, thickened duct walls, and sludge. Key association: ascending infection in an obstructed biliary system.
biliary-b26: Pneumobilia appears as echogenic linear foci within the liver that generate ring-down artifact because air is present in the bile ducts. Remember: branching central hepatic echoes with dirty artifact suggest biliary gas.
biliary-b27: Cholangiocarcinoma can cause malignant biliary obstruction, producing dilated ducts with an abrupt cutoff, along with pain, weight loss, and pruritus. Key fact: a sudden duct termination raises concern for an obstructing mass.
biliary-b28: A choledochal cyst is a congenital focal cystic dilatation of the common bile duct and may appear as an anechoic mass causing CBD enlargement, especially in infants or children. Remember: choledochal = cystic bile duct dilatation.
biliary-b29: Pruritus, weight loss, and elevated bilirubin are clinical findings of cholangiocarcinoma, whereas intrahepatic duct dilatation is an imaging finding rather than a clinical symptom/sign. Memory tip: 'clinical' refers to patient presentation and lab data, not sonographic appearance.
biliary-b30: Cholangiopneumonia is not a recognized cause of pneumobilia, whereas gastric surgery, fistula formation, and inflammatory biliary-enteric communications can introduce air into the biliary tree. Remember: pneumobilia usually results from surgery, instrumentation, or abnormal bowel-biliary connection.
pancreas-b1: Pancreatic divisum occurs when the dorsal and ventral ducts fail to fuse, so the short ventral duct drains mainly the pancreatic head rather than the whole gland. Remember: divisum = “division” of the duct systems.
pancreas-b2: Glucagon is an endocrine hormone made by the islet cells, not part of the pancreas’s exocrine digestive function. Remember: exocrine pancreas makes enzymes and bicarbonate; endocrine pancreas makes insulin and glucagon.
pancreas-b3: The accessory pancreatic duct is the duct of Santorini. Remember: Santorini = accessory duct, while Wirsung = main pancreatic duct.
pancreas-b4: Annular pancreas results from abnormal embryologic development that creates a ring of pancreatic tissue around the duodenum, causing obstruction. Remember: “annular” means ring-shaped.
pancreas-b5: von Hippel–Lindau disease is associated with pancreatic cysts and other cystic or vascular lesions. Remember: VHL commonly involves multiple organs, including the pancreas, kidneys, and CNS.
pancreas-b6: Adenocarcinoma is the most common pancreatic malignancy, arising from the exocrine ductal epithelium. Remember: when pancreatic cancer is mentioned clinically, it is usually ductal adenocarcinoma.
pancreas-b7: The Whipple procedure is classically performed for pancreatic carcinoma, especially tumors in the pancreatic head. Remember: Whipple = pancreaticoduodenectomy.
pancreas-b8: Sodium bicarbonate from the pancreas neutralizes acidic chyme entering the duodenum from the stomach. Remember: bicarbonate protects the small bowel and helps pancreatic enzymes function.
pancreas-b9: Pancreatic adenocarcinoma most commonly arises in the head of the pancreas. Remember: head lesions often cause obstructive jaundice by compressing the distal common bile duct.
pancreas-b10: A phlegmon is an inflammatory peripancreatic fluid collection associated with pancreatitis. Remember: phlegmon is inflamed soft tissue/fluid, whereas a pseudocyst is a more organized collection.
pancreas-b11: Focal pancreatitis most commonly involves the pancreatic head. Remember: the head is also the most common site for pancreatic adenocarcinoma, so imaging correlation is important.
pancreas-b12: A diffusely hypoechoic pancreas is more typical of acute pancreatitis due to edema, not chronic pancreatitis. Remember: chronic pancreatitis more often shows calcifications, ductal dilatation, and gland atrophy.
pancreas-b13: Biloma is least likely after pancreatic transplant because it is a bile leak collection, more typical of hepatobiliary surgery. Remember: pancreatic transplant complications more commonly include hematoma, ascites, or urinoma.
pancreas-b14: Weight gain is not a classic feature of acute pancreatitis; patients more often have severe pain, fever, and leukocytosis. Remember: acute pancreatitis typically presents with epigastric pain radiating to the back.
pancreas-b15: Lipase is more specific than amylase for acute pancreatitis and usually remains elevated longer. Remember: amylase can rise in several other abdominal conditions, but lipase points more strongly to pancreatic injury.
biliary-b46: Cholangiofluoroscopy is a fluoroscopic contrast study used to evaluate the biliary tree and often the pancreatic ductal system in the radiology/interventional setting. Remember: “fluoro” signals real-time x-ray imaging of ductal flow.
biliary-b47: Posthepatic jaundice results from obstruction after bile is formed, usually within the extrahepatic biliary system, so it is classically linked to biliary obstruction. Memory tip: posthepatic = problem after the liver, in the ducts.
biliary-b48: The sphincter of Oddi is also called the hepatopancreatic sphincter because it surrounds the distal common bile duct and pancreatic duct at their entry into the duodenum. Remember: hepato + pancreatic identifies both systems it controls.
biliary-b49: Just distal to the cystic duct insertion, the duct is called the common bile duct. Key anatomy fact: common hepatic duct + cystic duct = common bile duct.
biliary-b50: Pruritus is the medical term for severe itching and is common with cholestasis from retained bile salts. Remember: jaundice with itching should make you think pruritus from biliary disease.
biliary-b51: Simultaneous enlargement of the common bile duct and pancreatic duct is called the double-duct sign. High-yield memory aid: think of two obstructed ducts near the ampulla or pancreatic head.
biliary-b52: The triangular cord sign is associated with biliary atresia, not cholangitis. Cholangitis more often shows ductal dilatation, sludge, and sometimes stones causing obstruction.
biliary-b53: Sclerosing cholangitis is the most common risk factor listed for cholangiocarcinoma because chronic inflammation and fibrosis of the bile ducts predispose to malignancy. Remember: long-standing duct irritation raises cancer risk.
biliary-b54: Choledocholithiasis most commonly lodges near the ampulla of Vater, where the distal common bile duct narrows before entering the duodenum. Memory tip: stones often get stuck at narrow distal outlets.
biliary-b55: AIDS cholangitis occurs in severely immunocompromised patients and is linked to opportunistic infections such as Cryptosporidium and CMV. Remember: AIDS cholangitis = infectious biliary disease in advanced immunosuppression.
biliary-b56: Adenocarcinoma is the most common histologic type of cholangiocarcinoma because bile duct epithelium is glandular in origin. Memory aid: most GI and biliary tract cancers are adenocarcinomas.
biliary-b57: Ascariasis is transmitted by the fecal–oral route after ingestion of eggs from contaminated food, water, or soil. Remember: poor sanitation is the classic setting for Ascaris infection.
biliary-b58: Biliary atresia causes progressive obstruction of bile flow in infancy, leading to chronic cholestasis, fibrosis, and ultimately cirrhosis. Key fact: untreated biliary atresia is a major cause of pediatric liver failure.
biliary-b59: Bile duct sludge fits a patient with RUQ pain and fever when echogenic intraductal material is seen without definite shadowing like a stone. Remember: sludge is low-level echogenic debris within bile ducts or gallbladder.
biliary-b60: Cholesterol is the keyed major component of bile in this context and is clinically important because excess cholesterol contributes to cholesterol gallstone formation. Memory tip: supersaturated cholesterol bile promotes stones.
pancreas-b16: Exocrine enteric drainage is now more common because it is more physiologic and avoids many urologic complications seen with bladder drainage. Remember: transplanted pancreatic exocrine secretions are usually routed into bowel, not bladder.
pancreas-b17: The lesser sac is a classic and common location for pancreatic pseudocysts because it lies directly adjacent to the pancreas. Remember: pancreatic fluid often tracks into nearby spaces, especially the lesser sac behind the stomach.
pancreas-b18: Hepatitis is least likely because the major classic causes of acute pancreatitis are gallstones, alcohol abuse, and trauma. Remember the high-yield pancreatitis triad: gallstones, alcohol, and pancreatic injury/obstruction.
pancreas-b19: Insulinoma is the most common islet cell tumor and arises from beta cells that secrete insulin. Remember: the most common functioning pancreatic endocrine tumor causes hypoglycemia from excess insulin.
pancreas-b20: Amylase typically rises first in acute pancreatitis, often within hours of symptom onset, before lipase remains elevated longer. Remember: amylase rises early, lipase stays longer.
pancreas-b21: A painless enlarged gallbladder with jaundice (Courvoisier sign) suggests obstruction from a pancreatic head adenocarcinoma rather than stones. Remember: pancreatic head masses can compress the distal common bile duct.
pancreas-b22: A pancreatic gastrinoma causes Zollinger–Ellison syndrome by producing excess gastrin, leading to severe peptic ulcer disease. Remember: gastrinoma = gastrin excess = acid hypersecretion and recurrent ulcers.
pancreas-b23: The sphincter of Oddi is the muscular valve that regulates bile and pancreatic juice flow into the duodenum. Remember: Oddi controls the outlet; Vater refers to the ampulla, not the sphincter muscle.
pancreas-b24: The main pancreatic duct is the duct of Wirsung, which courses through the pancreas to join the common bile duct near the ampulla. Remember: Wirsung = main duct; Santorini = accessory duct.
pancreas-b25: Pancreatic adenocarcinoma commonly causes epigastric pain, weight loss, and jaundice, but decreased amylase and lipase are not typical findings. Remember: pancreatic cancer often obstructs ducts, so labs may be normal or increased, not characteristically decreased.
pancreas-b26: The head of the pancreas sits within the C-loop of the duodenum, making the duodenum the bowel segment that encompasses it. Remember: pancreatic head nests inside the duodenal loop.
pancreas-b27: Acinar cells perform the exocrine function by producing digestive enzymes released into the pancreatic ducts. Remember: acinar = enzyme-producing exocrine tissue; islets are the endocrine portion.
pancreas-b28: An acutely inflamed pancreas is most often hypoechoic because edema lowers its echogenicity. Remember: acute inflammation adds fluid, and fluid-rich tissue usually looks darker on ultrasound.
pancreas-b29: Splenic vein thrombosis is a well-known vascular complication of acute pancreatitis because the vein runs close to the pancreatic body and tail. Remember: pancreatitis can inflame or compress adjacent splenic vessels.
pancreas-b30: The head of the pancreas receives arterial supply primarily through the pancreaticoduodenal arcades, with major contribution from the gastroduodenal artery. Remember: GDA helps supply the pancreatic head; the splenic artery mainly serves body and tail.
pancreas-b46: Acute pancreatitis is most likely because back pain with elevated amylase is a classic presentation of acute pancreatic inflammation. Remember: acute pancreatitis often appears as an enlarged, hypoechoic pancreas on ultrasound.
pancreas-b47: Interstitial edematous pancreatitis is the most common form, characterized by diffuse inflammatory edema without major necrosis. Key memory aid: most acute pancreatitis cases are the milder edematous type, not hemorrhagic or necrotizing.
pancreas-b48: Hypertension is not part of the Whipple triad. The triad includes symptoms of hypoglycemia, low fasting glucose, and relief after glucose administration—think 'low sugar gets better with sugar.'
pancreas-b49: The Whipple triad points to insulinoma because this tumor causes episodic hypoglycemia that improves with glucose. Remember: insulin excess lowers blood sugar, producing the classic triad.
pancreas-b50: The islets of Langerhans perform the endocrine function by secreting hormones such as insulin and glucagon. Memory tip: islets = internal secretion; acinar cells handle the exocrine digestive enzymes.
pancreas-b51: The kidney is commonly transplanted at the same time as the pancreas, especially in patients with diabetes-related renal failure. Key fact: simultaneous pancreas-kidney transplant is a standard treatment combination in type 1 diabetes.
pancreas-b52: Pancreatic cysts are associated with cystic fibrosis because thick secretions obstruct ducts and promote cystic change. Remember: CF commonly affects exocrine glands, including the pancreas.
pancreas-b53: Amylase converts starch to sugar by breaking down complex carbohydrates into simpler sugars. Easy memory aid: amylase acts on amylose, a starch component.
pancreas-b54: Acute pancreatitis is best described as a hypoechoic, enlarged pancreas due to edema and inflammation. Remember: acute = swollen and dark; chronic = shrunken, bright, and calcified.
pancreas-b55: Chronic pancreatitis classically appears as an atrophic, hyperechoic gland with calcifications and a dilated main pancreatic duct. Key fact: fibrosis and calcification make the gland brighter and smaller over time.
pancreas-b56: Splenic vein thrombosis is a recognized vascular complication of acute pancreatitis because the vein runs close to the inflamed pancreatic body and tail. Remember this can lead to left-sided portal hypertension.
pancreas-b57: Pancreatic adenocarcinoma most commonly appears as a hypoechoic mass on ultrasound. Memory tip: a dark pancreatic mass with ductal dilatation should raise concern for adenocarcinoma.
pancreas-b58: The Whipple procedure is another name for pancreaticoduodenectomy, the operation used for many pancreatic head malignancies. Remember: it removes the pancreatic head along with the duodenum.
pancreas-b59: Periportal cuffing is least likely in acute pancreatitis, whereas pseudocyst and phlegmon are well-known complications and choledocholithiasis may be an associated cause. Think acute pancreatitis findings are centered around the pancreas and peripancreatic tissues.
pancreas-b60: The uncinate process lies posterior to the superior mesenteric vein. Key landmark: the uncinate hooks behind the mesenteric vessels, helping distinguish it from the pancreatic head.
pancreas-b31: Insulinomas are islet-cell tumors that secrete excess insulin, so the classic clinical finding is hypoglycemia. Remember Whipple’s triad: symptoms of hypoglycemia, low blood glucose, and relief after glucose.
pancreas-b32: Early acute pancreatitis may appear normal on ultrasound before edema and fluid changes become evident. Key fact: sonographic findings often lag behind symptoms and lab abnormalities such as elevated amylase/lipase.
pancreas-b33: Mucinous cystadenocarcinomas are most commonly found in the pancreatic body and tail, especially in middle-aged women. Memory tip: mucinous cystic neoplasms favor the distal pancreas.
pancreas-b34: Simultaneous dilatation/obstruction of the common bile duct and pancreatic duct is called the double-duct sign. This pattern strongly suggests a mass at the pancreatic head or ampulla.
pancreas-b35: Courvoisier gallbladder refers to a palpable distended gallbladder caused by extrahepatic biliary obstruction, often near the pancreatic head. Remember: painless jaundice plus a palpable gallbladder raises concern for malignancy.
pancreas-b36: The pancreas is primarily a retroperitoneal organ, lying posterior to the stomach. A helpful memory fact is that only the tail approaches the splenorenal ligament region, but the gland is still considered retroperitoneal.
pancreas-b37: The pancreatic head lies right of the SMV, anterior to the IVC, and inferior to the portal vein. Key landmark: the head sits within the C-loop of the duodenum.
pancreas-b38: The splenic vein courses along the posterior aspect of the pancreas and outlines the tail posteriorly. Memory tip: follow the splenic vein to help identify the body and tail of the pancreas.
pancreas-b39: The pancreatic neck lies directly anterior to the portal confluence, where the splenic vein and SMV join. This is a classic landmark used to identify the neck sonographically.
pancreas-b40: Insulin is the pancreatic hormone that promotes cellular glucose uptake and storage, counteracting glucagon’s effect. Remember: insulin lowers blood glucose, while glucagon raises it.
pancreas-b41: Acinar cells are the exocrine cells of the pancreas that produce digestive enzymes such as amylase and lipase. Memory aid: acinar = enzyme-producing, islet cells = hormone-producing.
pancreas-b42: The pancreatic tail extends toward the spleen and lies medial to the splenic hilum. A useful landmark is that the tail often points toward the left kidney and splenic hilum.
pancreas-b43: Hyperparathyroidism can raise serum calcium levels, and hypercalcemia is a known risk factor for chronic pancreatitis. Remember: alcohol is most common overall, but metabolic causes like hypercalcemia also matter.
pancreas-b44: In a patient with weight loss, palpable gallbladder, and elevated ALP, a dilated main pancreatic duct is a key finding suggesting pancreatic head obstruction. Remember: ductal dilatation plus jaundice-like labs supports the double-duct pattern.
pancreas-b45: Given the history of weight loss and Courvoisier-type findings, the measured lesion is most consistent with pancreatic adenocarcinoma. Key fact: adenocarcinoma most often arises in the pancreatic head and obstructs both ducts.
spleen-b1: A chronic splenic hematoma can calcify over time after prior trauma and may produce clean posterior acoustic shadowing. Remember: a remote trauma history plus calcified splenic mass strongly suggests an old organized hematoma.
spleen-b2: A small mass near the splenic hilum that is isoechoic to the spleen is most consistent with a splenunculus, or accessory spleen. Key fact: accessory spleens are commonly found at the splenic hilum and match normal splenic echotexture.
spleen-b3: Angiosarcoma is the rare malignant vascular tumor of the spleen. Remember: hemangioma is benign, while angiosarcoma is its aggressive malignant vascular counterpart.
spleen-b4: A splenic infarct classically appears as a wedge-shaped hypoechoic peripheral lesion in a patient with acute LUQ pain. Key fact: infarcts follow the splenic arterial distribution, creating the triangular or wedge configuration.
spleen-b5: A wandering spleen is abnormally mobile because of lax or absent supporting ligaments, which increases the risk of pedicle twisting. Remember: the major complication of a wandering spleen is splenic torsion.
spleen-b6: Splenic hemangiomas are most commonly hyperechoic on ultrasound. Key fact: like many benign vascular lesions, their bright echogenic appearance is a classic clue.
spleen-b7: Erythropoiesis is the production of red blood cells. Remember: 'erythro-' means red and '-poiesis' means formation.
spleen-b8: Healed granulomatous infection such as toxoplasmosis can leave multiple tiny echogenic foci scattered throughout the spleen. Key fact: granulomas often calcify, making them appear bright on sonography.
spleen-b9: The splenic artery courses along the superior border of the pancreatic body and tail, making it an important landmark. Remember: on ultrasound, the tortuous splenic artery helps identify the pancreas superiorly.
spleen-b10: Portal hypertension is the most common cause of splenomegaly because elevated portal venous pressure leads to congestive enlargement of the spleen. Key fact: splenomegaly commonly accompanies portal-system venous congestion.
spleen-b11: Splenic hamartomas are benign lesions that have been associated with tuberous sclerosis. Remember this association as part of the hamartoma-forming tendency seen in tuberous sclerosis.
spleen-b12: The red pulp is responsible for the spleen’s phagocytic filtering function, removing old or abnormal blood cells. Key fact: white pulp is mainly lymphoid tissue for immune activity, while red pulp handles filtration.
spleen-b13: A small rounded echogenic splenic mass without shadowing is most typical of a hemangioma. Remember: hemangiomas are the most common benign primary splenic neoplasm and are often echogenic.
spleen-b14: A lymphangioma is a benign congenital malformation of the lymphatic system. Key fact: it is a developmental lesion rather than a true malignant neoplasm.
spleen-b15: The spleen is an intraperitoneal organ located in the left upper quadrant. Remember: it is suspended by peritoneal ligaments, unlike retroperitoneal structures such as the kidneys.
spleen-b16: White pulp contains lymphoid tissue surrounding arterioles and is responsible for the spleen’s immune/lymphatic role. Remember: white pulp = immunity, while red pulp mainly filters blood cells.
spleen-b17: Sickle cell anemia is most common in people of African, Mediterranean, and Middle Eastern ancestry, so a Caucasian child is least likely to be affected. Key memory aid: the trait is linked to malaria-endemic populations.
spleen-b18: The splenic vein courses along the posterior surface of the pancreatic body and tail, making it an important landmark on sonography. Remember: artery is usually superior and tortuous, vein is posterior.
spleen-b19: The spleen stores iron, serves as a blood reservoir, and helps defend against disease, but it does not destroy phagocytic cells. Key fact: splenic macrophages are the phagocytic cells that remove aged blood cells.
spleen-b20: Repeated sickle cell infarctions can progressively shrink and scar the spleen until only a small remnant remains, called autosplenectomy. Remember: the spleen essentially self-destructs from recurrent vascular occlusion.
spleen-b21: The splenic hilum is the most common site of an accessory spleen because it forms near the main spleen during embryologic development. Key fact: accessory spleens are usually small, round, and isoechoic to splenic tissue.
spleen-b22: Splenomegaly is commonly associated with trauma, hemolytic disorders, and mononucleosis, but pancreatitis is not a typical cause. Remember: spleen enlargement often reflects hematologic, infectious, or portal venous conditions.
spleen-b23: Pitting is the splenic process that removes inclusions or unwanted material from red blood cells without destroying the cell. Memory aid: pitting = picking debris out; culling = removing the whole cell.
spleen-b24: Diffuse splenic involvement by lymphoma or leukemia commonly enlarges the spleen, producing splenomegaly. Key fact: hematologic malignancies often infiltrate the spleen diffusely rather than as a single focal mass.
spleen-b25: The splenic artery arises from the celiac trunk, one of its three major branches. Remember the celiac trifecta: left gastric, common hepatic, and splenic arteries.
spleen-b26: A splenic cleft is a congenital anomaly where a band or notch divides the spleen into two portions. Key fact: clefts are developmental and can mimic lacerations if the history is unclear.
spleen-b27: Histoplasmosis commonly causes multiple splenic granulomas, often seen as calcified focal lesions. Remember: granulomatous infections such as histoplasmosis and TB frequently leave calcified splenic scars.
spleen-b28: After blunt trauma, a complex splenic mass most likely represents a hematoma from hemorrhage within or around the spleen. Key fact: traumatic hematomas can appear echogenic early and become more complex over time.
spleen-b29: A sickle cell crisis often causes vascular congestion and sequestration in the spleen, leading to splenomegaly, especially earlier in the disease. Remember: repeated crises may later progress to autosplenectomy.
spleen-b30: Epstein–Barr virus is a herpesvirus and the classic cause of infectious mononucleosis. Key memory fact: mono commonly produces splenomegaly, which is why patients are warned about splenic rupture risk.
spleen-b46: A chronic splenic infarct classically becomes a peripheral wedge-shaped hyperechoic lesion from fibrosis and scarring. Remember: acute infarcts are often hypoechoic, while chronic infarcts turn brighter over time.
spleen-b47: Bacteremia can seed the spleen hematogenously, making a splenic abscess the key risk. Remember: pyogenic abscesses often occur with fever, LUQ pain, and systemic infection.
spleen-b48: Hemangioma is the most common benign splenic neoplasm. Remember: it is also a common benign vascular tumor in other organs, especially the liver.
spleen-b49: Granulomas are commonly linked to chronic granulomatous diseases like TB, histoplasmosis, and sarcoidosis, not bacterial endocarditis. Remember: splenic granulomas often calcify and may appear as echogenic foci.
spleen-b50: Dirty shadowing suggests gas within a lesion, which strongly supports a pyogenic splenic abscess. Remember: gas-forming organisms create reverberation/dirty shadowing rather than clean acoustic shadowing.
spleen-b51: Hodgkin lymphoma generally has a better treatment response and recovery rate than many other splenic malignancies. Remember: lymphoma is the most common malignant process involving the spleen.
spleen-b52: Sickle cell anemia increases hemolysis, which raises bilirubin production and predisposes patients to pigment gallstones. Remember: hemolytic diseases commonly lead to gallstone formation.
spleen-b53: The spleen lies in the left upper quadrant posterolateral to the stomach. Remember: it also sits just beneath the left hemidiaphragm and lateral to the left kidney.
spleen-b54: In a patient with acute LUQ pain and sickle cell disease, splenic infarct is the most likely diagnosis because vaso-occlusion commonly compromises splenic blood flow. Remember: infarcts are often peripheral and wedge-shaped.
spleen-b55: Hepatofugal portal venous flow suggests portal hypertension, which fits a patient with ascites, jaundice, and splenomegaly. Remember: hepatofugal means flow is reversed, away from the liver.
spleen-b56: Heterotaxia syndromes are classically associated with congenital heart disease and polysplenia. Remember: polysplenia is a laterality abnormality involving multiple small spleens.
spleen-b57: Histoplasmosis is a fungal infection acquired by inhaling airborne spores. Remember: it can lead to calcified granulomas in the spleen, liver, and lungs.
spleen-b58: The gastrosplenic ligament connects the spleen to the stomach. Remember: it carries the short gastric vessels and helps support the spleen in the LUQ.
spleen-b59: A normal spleen is typically slightly more echogenic than the liver on ultrasound. Remember: comparing splenic echogenicity to the liver is a quick normal reference during scanning.
spleen-b60: Leukopenia means a decreased number of white blood cells. Remember: 'leuko-' refers to white and '-penia' means deficiency.
spleen-b31: Culling is the spleen’s removal of aged or abnormally shaped red blood cells from circulation. Remember: culling = whole-cell removal, whereas pitting removes only intracellular inclusions from otherwise viable RBCs.
spleen-b32: A splenic infarct is an area of ischemic necrosis caused by loss of blood supply and oxygen. Key memory fact: infarcts in the spleen are often classically wedge-shaped on imaging.
spleen-b33: Sarcoidosis is a systemic granulomatous disease that can produce granulomas in the spleen and many other organs. Remember: noncaseating granulomas are the hallmark finding of sarcoidosis.
spleen-b34: A hydatid cyst is a parasitic cyst caused by tapeworm infestation, most commonly Echinococcus. Memory tip: 'hydatid' should make you think of echinococcal parasitic disease and complex cysts.
spleen-b35: Splenic hemangiomas are commonly incidental findings and most patients have no symptoms. Key fact: they are the most common benign primary neoplasm of the spleen.
spleen-b36: Reed–Sternberg cells are the classic pathologic marker of Hodgkin lymphoma. Remember: when you see Reed–Sternberg, think Hodgkin first.
spleen-b37: Splenosis is autotransplantation of splenic tissue, often after splenic rupture or splenectomy. Memory fact: unlike congenital accessory spleens, splenosis is acquired after trauma.
spleen-b38: This statement is false because the spleen actually has a concave medial/superior surface with splenic notches on the superior border, not the reversed contour described here. Remember: the splenic hilum lies on the concave visceral surface.
spleen-b39: The portal vein forms posterior to the pancreatic neck where the splenic vein joins the superior mesenteric vein. Key memory aid: portal vein = SV + SMV.
spleen-b40: Multiple small echogenic splenic foci most often represent benign granulomas, usually from prior healed granulomatous infection. Remember: these often calcify and appear bright on ultrasound.
spleen-b41: Extramedullary erythropoiesis is not a typical classic association tested for splenomegaly compared with conditions like cirrhosis or trauma-related enlargement. Memory tip: portal hypertension from cirrhosis commonly causes splenic enlargement.
spleen-b42: Angiosarcoma is the primary malignant tumor of the spleen. Remember: it is a rare but aggressive vascular malignancy with risk of spontaneous rupture.
spleen-b43: Fungal abscesses can produce a target or 'bull’s-eye' appearance in the spleen. Key fact: in immunocompromised patients, multiple small target lesions strongly suggest fungal infection.
spleen-b44: A splenic cyst is the best match because it typically appears as a well-defined anechoic lesion with posterior acoustic enhancement. Remember: simple cysts are fluid-filled and usually have thin, smooth walls.
spleen-b45: Splenic hamartoma is least likely because hamartomas are usually solid splenic masses, not cystic lesions like the abnormality in Figure 6-15. Memory fact: cystic splenic lesions are more associated with trauma, hydatid disease, or systemic cystic disorders.
urinary-b1: CRF typically shows small, echogenic kidneys with cortical thinning and poor corticomedullary differentiation. A good memory tip: chronic renal disease shrinks and scars the kidneys over time.
urinary-b2: Diabetes mellitus is the most common cause of chronic renal failure because long-term hyperglycemia damages the glomeruli. Remember: diabetic nephropathy is a leading cause of end-stage renal disease.
urinary-b3: A Skene gland cyst arises from the paraurethral glands, so it is located within or adjacent to the female urethra. Memory fact: Skene glands are the female homolog of the prostate.
urinary-b4: An angiomyolipoma is a classic incidental, usually echogenic renal mass found in an asymptomatic patient. Key fact: its fat content makes it appear very bright on ultrasound.
urinary-b5: ADPKD causes bilaterally enlarged kidneys with numerous cysts and is associated with renal failure, UTIs, and palpable abdominal masses in adults. Remember: ADPKD is the common adult polycystic kidney disease.
urinary-b6: Urinary tract infection is commonly associated with ADPKD because distorted cystic kidneys predispose to infection. Memory tip: cysts can become infected or bleed in polycystic kidney disease.
urinary-b7: Hypernephroma, or renal cell carcinoma, fits the classic history of hematuria, flank pain, and smoking in an older adult. Key fact: smoking is a major risk factor for RCC.
urinary-b8: LDH is especially helpful because renal infarction causes tissue necrosis, which releases lactate dehydrogenase into the blood. Remember: infarction often elevates LDH disproportionately.
urinary-b9: Nephrotic syndrome results from glomerular damage causing heavy proteinuria, which lowers oncotic pressure and leads to edema. Memory fact: nephrotic syndrome is classically linked with protein loss and swelling.
urinary-b10: A staghorn calculus is a hallmark finding in xanthogranulomatous pyelonephritis because chronic obstruction and infection are central to the disease. Remember: XGP often destroys the kidney around a large stone.
urinary-b11: Medullary nephrocalcinosis appears as increased echogenicity or calcification in the renal pyramids. Key fact: think 'medulla = pyramids,' where calcium deposition commonly occurs.
urinary-b12: Pyonephritis is least likely because medullary nephrocalcinosis is more commonly associated with metabolic disorders like hypercalcemia and hyperparathyroidism than with pus-producing infection. Memory tip: nephrocalcinosis usually reflects calcium imbalance.
urinary-b13: Renal artery stenosis is the most common vascular complication after renal transplantation and can lead to hypertension or graft dysfunction. Remember: evaluate transplant renal artery velocities when stenosis is suspected.
urinary-b14: Megacystis, or marked bladder enlargement from urinary tract obstruction, is the most common cause of prune belly syndrome. Key fact: obstruction leads to abdominal wall laxity and urinary tract dilation.
urinary-b15: Wilms tumor is another name for nephroblastoma, the most common primary renal malignancy in children. Memory tip: 'blastoma' helps identify it as an embryonal pediatric tumor.
urinary-b16: Beckwith–Wiedemann syndrome is a recognized pediatric overgrowth syndrome associated with increased Wilms tumor risk. Remember: Wilms tumor classically affects young children, often under age 5.
urinary-b17: Renal vein entrapment in nutcracker anatomy occurs when the left renal vein is compressed between the abdominal aorta and the superior mesenteric artery. Think: the vein is “cracked” in the aortomesenteric angle.
