urinary-b18: Nutcracker syndrome classically involves compression of the left renal vein, leading to venous hypertension and possible hematuria. Memory tip: the left renal vein crosses anterior to the aorta, making it vulnerable.
urinary-b19: Transitional cell carcinoma typically arises from the renal pelvis/collecting system and often presents with gross hematuria. Key fact: unlike most renal cell tumors, TCC is usually a central rather than cortical renal mass.
urinary-b20: The kidneys produce renin, which activates the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system to help regulate blood pressure. Remember: juxtaglomerular cells release renin when renal perfusion falls.
urinary-b21: Henoch–Schönlein purpura is a childhood autoimmune vasculitis that causes palpable purple skin lesions and can involve the kidneys. Key memory fact: it is an IgA-mediated small-vessel disease.
urinary-b22: The nephron is the kidney’s functional unit because it filters blood and forms urine. Remember: each nephron includes a glomerulus and tubules working together.
urinary-b23: A renal-to-aortic peak systolic velocity ratio greater than 3.5 is a classic Doppler criterion for significant renal artery stenosis. Memory tip: compare the renal artery speed to the aorta to screen for narrowing.
urinary-b24: The kidneys are retroperitoneal organs, located behind the peritoneal cavity along the posterior abdominal wall. Remember: most urinary tract structures are retroperitoneal.
urinary-b25: The fibrous protective covering directly surrounding the kidney is the renal capsule. Key fact: Glisson capsule belongs to the liver, not the kidney.
urinary-b26: The left renal vein normally courses anterior to the aorta and posterior to the superior mesenteric artery. This relationship is important because it is the vessel compressed in nutcracker syndrome.
urinary-b27: Hypotension is not a typical feature of renal transplant failure; more common findings include oliguria, proteinuria, and elevated creatinine. Remember: failing graft function usually raises waste markers rather than lowering blood pressure.
urinary-b28: Compensatory hypertrophy describes enlargement of the functioning kidney when the opposite kidney is absent or poorly functioning. Memory tip: the remaining kidney grows to handle the extra workload.
urinary-b29: A dromedary hump is a benign bulge on the lateral border of the left kidney caused by splenic impression. Remember: it mimics a mass but has normal cortical echogenicity.
urinary-b30: A duplicated collecting system is the most common congenital urinary tract anomaly. Key fact: duplication may be partial or complete and often involves a bifid pelvis or duplicated ureter.
urinary-b31: A renal scar typically appears as an echogenic band extending from the renal sinus into the parenchyma, reflecting fibrotic tissue. Remember: scarring often causes cortical thinning and contour deformity, especially after chronic reflux or infection.
urinary-b32: The pelvis is the most common site for an ectopic kidney because ascent from the fetal pelvis fails during development. Remember: ectopic kidneys are often malrotated and may have shorter ureters.
urinary-b33: In acute renal failure, BUN and creatinine usually rise, not fall, because the kidneys cannot adequately clear nitrogenous waste. Remember: oliguria plus elevated BUN/creatinine is a classic ARF pattern.
urinary-b34: With complete ureteral duplication, the upper pole moiety is prone to obstruction from a ureterocele. Remember the Weigert-Meyer rule: upper pole obstructs, lower pole refluxes.
urinary-b35: Diabetes mellitus is the most common cause of chronic renal failure due to progressive diabetic nephropathy. Remember: long-standing hyperglycemia damages glomeruli and gradually reduces renal function.
urinary-b36: Acquired renal cystic disease develops in patients with chronic renal failure on long-term hemodialysis. Remember: dialysis-associated kidneys often become small and cystic, with increased RCC risk.
urinary-b37: Chronic renal failure usually produces kidneys that are smaller and more echogenic from fibrosis and loss of normal tissue. Remember: bright, shrunken kidneys are a classic chronic disease appearance.
urinary-b38: Exophytic cysts project outward from the renal surface away from the kidney. Remember: 'exo-' means outside, helping distinguish them from central peripelvic or parapelvic cysts.
urinary-b39: Normal kidneys with urinary symptoms and a thickened bladder wall in a distended bladder most strongly suggest cystitis. Remember: bladder wall thicker than about 3 mm when distended is abnormal.
urinary-b40: von Hippel–Lindau syndrome is associated with CNS and orbital tumors, renal cysts, and adrenal tumors such as pheochromocytoma. Remember: VHL also carries a strong risk for renal cell carcinoma.
urinary-b41: Transitional cell carcinoma most commonly arises in the renal pelvis because it develops from urothelium lining the collecting system. Remember: TCC follows the urinary tract lining from renal pelvis to bladder.
urinary-b42: Acute tubular necrosis is the most common cause of acute renal failure, usually from ischemia or nephrotoxic injury. Remember: ATN is an intrinsic renal cause and often follows shock, sepsis, or toxins.
urinary-b43: Smooth walls are a feature of a simple cyst, not a complex cyst. Remember: complex cysts show suspicious features such as internal echoes, septations, or mural nodules.
urinary-b44: A hemorrhagic renal cyst can cause hematuria because bleeding into or from the cyst may communicate with the collecting system. Remember: blood products also create internal echoes, making the cyst complex.
urinary-b45: Angiomyolipoma is the most common solid renal mass and is typically very echogenic because of its fat content. Remember: AML is benign and classically associated with tuberous sclerosis.
urinary-b46: Infantile polycystic kidney disease is another name for autosomal recessive polycystic kidney disease (ARPKD). Remember: ARPKD typically presents in infancy/childhood, while ADPKD more often presents in adulthood.
urinary-b47: ARPKD classically appears as bilaterally enlarged, diffusely echogenic kidneys because of innumerable tiny cysts that reduce corticomedullary differentiation. Key memory aid: ARPKD = enlarged bright baby kidneys.
urinary-b48: Tuberous sclerosis is a multisystem disorder associated with seizures/epilepsy and renal angiomyolipomas. Remember: tuberous sclerosis commonly causes benign hamartomas in multiple organs, especially brain and kidneys.
urinary-b49: Most simple renal cysts cause no symptoms and are found incidentally on imaging. Key fact: a simple cyst is typically anechoic, thin-walled, and shows posterior acoustic enhancement.
urinary-b50: Renal cortical thinning is suspected when the cortex measures less than 1 cm. Remember: the cortex should normally be thicker; thinning suggests chronic renal parenchymal disease.
urinary-b51: A ureteral stricture is an intrinsic obstructing lesion within the ureter, not an external compressive cause. Key memory aid: extrinsic hydronephrosis comes from outside pressure, such as pregnancy or pelvic masses.
urinary-b52: Peritoneal dialysis commonly leaves dialysate fluid in the abdomen, so ascites is a frequent sonographic finding. Remember: the peritoneal cavity is used as the dialysis space.
urinary-b53: Pyonephrosis means pus within an obstructed renal collecting system. Key fact: think 'pyo' = pus; it is more specific than pyelonephritis, which is infection/inflammation of the kidney itself.
urinary-b54: Candida albicans is the most common organism causing fungal urinary tract infections. Remember: Candida is especially common in immunocompromised, diabetic, or catheterized patients.
urinary-b55: Glomerulonephritis commonly causes proteinuria, azotemia, and may follow a throat infection, but hypercalcemia is not a typical feature. Key memory aid: GN is a glomerular inflammatory process, not a calcium disorder.
urinary-b56: Urethritis is inflammation of the urethra and is not a typical intrinsic obstructive cause of hydronephrosis. Remember: intrinsic hydronephrosis usually results from a structural blockage like stones, UPJ obstruction, or ureterocele.
urinary-b57: Nephrocalcinosis is associated with UTIs, stones, and metabolic disorders such as hyperparathyroidism, but weight loss is not a classic finding. Key fact: nephrocalcinosis refers to calcium deposition in the renal parenchyma.
urinary-b58: ADPKD is associated with extrarenal cysts, especially in the liver and sometimes the pancreas. Remember: ADPKD is a systemic cystic disorder, unlike MCDK, which is usually limited to one kidney.
urinary-b59: A staghorn calculus is a large branching stone that fills the renal pelvis and often extends into the calyces. Key memory aid: it is named for its antler-like shape.
urinary-b60: The ureterovesical junction is the most common site where a urinary stone becomes lodged because it is one of the narrowest parts of the ureter. Remember the three narrowing points: UPJ, pelvic brim, and UVJ.
adrenal-b1: Adrenal hemorrhage is most likely in a stressed newborn after birth anoxia, especially with jaundice and a triangular heterogeneous suprarenal mass. Neonatal adrenal hemorrhage commonly occurs on the right and may mimic a solid mass early on.
adrenal-b2: Thinning arms and legs is more characteristic of Cushing syndrome from cortisol excess, not Conn syndrome. Conn syndrome is hyperaldosteronism, classically causing hypertension, hypokalemia, polyuria, and excessive thirst.
adrenal-b3: Hematocrit is most useful because internal bleeding lowers the percentage of red blood cells in circulating blood. A falling hematocrit is a key clue to hemorrhage, especially when correlated with clinical instability.
adrenal-b4: Adrenal rests are ectopic adrenal tissue that can occur in the testes and are associated with congenital adrenal hyperplasia. Remember: CAH can stimulate these rests, making them appear as bilateral testicular masses.
adrenal-b5: Cushing syndrome is associated with excess cortisol, producing hypertension, hyperglycemia, central obesity, and sometimes an adrenal mass. Think 'too much cortisol' for the classic body habitus and metabolic changes.
adrenal-b6: This is the exception because adrenal glands are endocrine, not exocrine, glands. Endocrine glands secrete hormones directly into the bloodstream, while exocrine glands use ducts.
adrenal-b7: Gerota fascia is the connective tissue layer enclosing the kidneys and adrenal glands. A helpful memory point: the adrenals sit within the perirenal space, bounded by Gerota fascia.
adrenal-b8: The left suprarenal vein drains into the left renal vein, whereas the right suprarenal vein drains directly into the IVC. This side-to-side asymmetry is a favorite anatomy fact to remember.
adrenal-b9: Conn syndrome (primary hyperaldosteronism) results from excess aldosterone, usually from an adrenal adenoma. Remember: hypertension with hypokalemia and hypernatremia; Cushing syndrome is the one caused by excess cortisol.
adrenal-b10: With active internal hemorrhage, hematocrit decreases as blood loss reduces circulating red cell volume. Trend matters: serial drops in hematocrit are more informative than a single value.
adrenal-b11: Hypercortisolism causes the classic Cushingoid appearance, including a buffalo hump and moon face. Excess cortisol redistributes fat centrally, which helps distinguish it from other adrenal disorders.
adrenal-b12: Endocrine glands release hormones directly into the bloodstream without ducts. The adrenal glands are endocrine organs, which is why their hormones have widespread systemic effects.
adrenal-b13: A hematoma is a localized collection of blood, often forming after trauma or hemorrhage. On ultrasound, its appearance changes over time as the blood ages and organizes.
adrenal-b14: Cushing disease specifically results from an ACTH-secreting anterior pituitary tumor. Key memory aid: Cushing disease is pituitary, while Cushing syndrome is the broader state of cortisol excess.
adrenal-b15: The adrenal glands receive arterial blood from the suprarenal arteries: superior, middle, and inferior suprarenal branches. Remember, despite their small size, the adrenals have a rich vascular supply.
adrenal-b16: Addison disease causes primary adrenal insufficiency, and increased ACTH can stimulate melanocytes, producing the classic bronze skin pigmentation. Memory tip: Addison = "add pigment" plus low cortisol/aldosterone.
adrenal-b17: Hyperfunctioning adrenal adenomas commonly cause endocrine syndromes like Cushing or Conn syndrome and may appear as an adrenal mass, but an acute drop in hematocrit suggests hemorrhage, not adenoma. Think hematocrit drop = bleeding.
adrenal-b18: Addison disease is the classic term for primary adrenocortical insufficiency, meaning the adrenal cortex itself fails to produce adequate hormones. Remember: primary problem in the adrenal gland = Addison disease.
adrenal-b19: Adrenaline is produced by the adrenal medulla, not the cortex. The cortex makes steroid hormones—cortisol, aldosterone, and androgens—so remember: cortex = salt, sugar, sex.
adrenal-b20: Norepinephrine is a catecholamine made by the adrenal medulla. A quick memory aid: medulla handles the fight-or-flight chemicals, while the cortex makes steroid hormones.
adrenal-b21: Hyponatremia literally means low sodium in the blood: "hypo" = low, "natri" = sodium, and "-emia" = blood condition. This term is commonly linked with adrenal insufficiency.
adrenal-b22: Epinephrine and norepinephrine are the catecholamines that drive the sympathetic fight-or-flight response. Remember: adrenal medulla releases these fast-acting stress hormones.
adrenal-b23: Addison disease causes low aldosterone, which leads to sodium loss and therefore hyponatremia. Memory tip: Addison = low salt, low pressure, and often hyperpigmentation.
adrenal-b24: The right adrenal gland lies posterior and lateral to the IVC, an important landmark during sonographic scanning. Remember: on the right, find the IVC first, then look just behind and lateral to it.
adrenal-b25: An anechoic lesion with posterior acoustic enhancement superior and medial to the right kidney is most consistent with an adrenal cyst. Simple cysts are fluid-filled, so they appear black with through transmission.
adrenal-b26: The right suprarenal vein drains directly into the IVC, unlike the left suprarenal vein, which usually drains into the left renal vein. Memory tip: right adrenal vein = short, straight to the IVC.
adrenal-b27: Pheochromocytoma is a catecholamine-secreting adrenal medullary tumor classically associated with severe hypertension, tachycardia, and tremors. Think "pheo" = episodic surges of adrenaline-like symptoms.
adrenal-b28: This body habitus and hypertension suggest Cushing syndrome, which is commonly caused by a hyperfunctioning adrenal adenoma. Remember the classic pattern: central obesity with thin extremities points to excess cortisol.
adrenal-b29: Pheochromocytomas most commonly appear as hyperechoic adrenal masses on sonography. A useful memory point is that these adrenal medullary tumors are often associated with dramatic hypertension.
adrenal-b30: Neuroblastoma is the most common extracranial malignant mass in children and often arises in the adrenal region. Remember: pediatric adrenal malignancy = think neuroblastoma first.
adrenal-b46: An adrenal adenoma is a common incidental adrenal mass and may be discovered during evaluation for unrelated problems such as elevated liver function tests. Remember: adenomas are the most frequent benign adrenal neoplasm in adults.
adrenal-b47: Pheochromocytoma classically presents with episodic headaches, anxiety, and excessive sweating from catecholamine excess. Remember the triad: headache, palpitations, and diaphoresis suggests a functioning adrenal medullary tumor.
adrenal-b48: Conn syndrome is primary hyperaldosteronism, which causes polyuria from sodium and water imbalance. Remember: Conn = too much aldosterone, classically linked with hypertension and altered potassium levels.
adrenal-b49: Hirsutism means excessive terminal hair growth in women in androgen-dependent areas where hair is normally minimal. Remember: it reflects androgen excess and is different from generalized increased hair growth.
adrenal-b50: Hypernatremia literally means an abnormally high sodium concentration in the blood. Remember: 'natr-' refers to sodium, while 'kal-' refers to potassium.
adrenal-b51: Cushing syndrome causes hypercortisolism, producing classic abdominal striae from skin thinning and stretching. Remember: purple abdominal striae are a hallmark physical finding of cortisol excess.
adrenal-b52: Hyperkalemia means an elevated potassium level in the blood. Remember: 'kalemia' refers to potassium, so hyperkalemia = high K+.
adrenal-b53: This presentation is most consistent with Addison disease, and the adrenal glands may appear enlarged, especially in primary adrenal involvement. Remember: hyperpigmentation points to primary adrenal insufficiency because ACTH is elevated.
adrenal-b54: Neuroblastoma is the most likely adrenal mass in a young child with abdominal pain and weight loss. Remember: neuroblastoma is the most common extracranial solid malignancy of childhood and often arises in the adrenal medulla.
adrenal-b55: In a newborn with anemia, jaundice, and hypotension, an adrenal hematoma is the classic diagnosis. Remember: neonatal adrenal hemorrhage commonly follows birth stress or trauma and can mimic a suprarenal mass.
adrenal-b56: The crura of the diaphragm are the tendinous extensions that anchor the diaphragm to the lumbar vertebral column. Remember: the right crus is usually longer than the left.
adrenal-b57: The adrenal cortex has three true zones: glomerulosa, fasciculata, and reticularis; zona pellucida is not one of them. Remember the cortex layers as GFR: glomerulosa, fasciculata, reticularis.
adrenal-b58: Addison disease is chronic primary hypoadrenalism caused by failure of the adrenal cortex. Remember: primary adrenal insufficiency leads to low cortisol and often hyperpigmentation.
adrenal-b59: Striae is the medical term for stretch marks. Remember: abdominal striae are commonly associated with rapid stretching or Cushing syndrome.
adrenal-b60: A chronic adrenal hematoma often calcifies over time, creating a calcified mass with posterior acoustic shadowing. Remember: acute hemorrhage changes appearance with age, but chronic lesions commonly become calcified.
adrenal-b31: Conn syndrome causes excess aldosterone, which increases renal sodium reabsorption and can lead to hypernatremia. Remember: aldosterone makes the body “hold salt,” and water follows sodium.
adrenal-b32: Neuroblastoma most often appears as a heterogeneous adrenal/suprarenal mass with calcifications on sonography. A key clue is that calcification is common in neuroblastoma, unlike many benign adrenal lesions.
adrenal-b33: Neuroblastoma typically presents in early childhood, most often before age 5 years. Remember: it is one of the classic adrenal-region malignancies of young children.
adrenal-b34: Aldosterone regulates blood pressure by controlling sodium retention and water balance in the kidneys. Key memory fact: more aldosterone means more sodium kept, so blood volume and pressure rise.
adrenal-b35: ACTH from the anterior pituitary stimulates the adrenal cortex to release its hormones. Remember the pituitary–adrenal link: ACTH drives cortisol production.
adrenal-b36: Neuroblastoma is the exception because it is a malignant pediatric adrenal/sympathetic tumor, not a benign adrenal mass. A helpful clue is its frequent association with calcifications and aggressive behavior.
adrenal-b37: Pheochromocytoma usually causes catecholamine excess symptoms like severe hypertension, sweating, and tremors, not bradycardia. Remember: excess epinephrine/norepinephrine typically increases heart rate.
adrenal-b38: Androgens are responsible for the development of male characteristics and are produced in part by the adrenal cortex. Key fact: the zona reticularis secretes adrenal androgens.
adrenal-b39: The adrenal glands receive blood from superior, middle, and inferior suprarenal arteries—from the inferior phrenic arteries, aorta, and renal arteries—not the celiac trunk. Remember the classic triad of adrenal arterial supply.
adrenal-b40: This statement is false because the left adrenal gland lies medial, not lateral, to the upper pole of the left kidney. Memory tip: both adrenals sit superomedial to their respective kidneys.
adrenal-b41: Congenital adrenal hyperplasia is associated with enzyme defects that impair cortisol production by the adrenal gland. Remember: low cortisol leads to increased ACTH stimulation and adrenal enlargement.
adrenal-b42: Pheochromocytoma is least likely because it arises from the adrenal medulla, not the cortex, and overproduces catecholamines rather than cortical hormones. Key distinction: cortex makes steroids; medulla makes epinephrine/norepinephrine.
adrenal-b43: An incidental adrenal mass found during imaging for unrelated reasons is called an incidentaloma. Remember: “incidental” finding + “-oma” for mass.
adrenal-b44: Cortisol is the major glucocorticoid produced by the adrenal cortex. A quick memory aid: glucocorticoids affect glucose metabolism, and cortisol is the primary one.
adrenal-b45: Neuroblastoma can present with bone pain from metastases and purple skin lesions in infants/children. Remember: this pediatric tumor often spreads early, especially to bone and skin.
vasculature-b1: The yin–yang sign is the bidirectional red-and-blue swirling color-flow pattern seen within a sac, classic for turbulent circulation. Remember: it looks like the yin–yang symbol because blood is moving in opposite directions during the cardiac cycle.
vasculature-b2: A pseudoaneurysm produces the yin–yang sign because blood enters and exits a contained arterial leak, creating swirling bidirectional flow. Key memory fact: pseudoaneurysms often also show a "to-and-fro" Doppler waveform at the neck.
vasculature-b3: The IVC lies anterior to the spine and typically to the right of the midline, adjacent to the abdominal aorta. Memory tip: on transverse imaging, the aorta is left and thicker-walled; the IVC is right and more compressible.
vasculature-b4: Femoral artery pseudoaneurysms commonly occur after heart catheterization from arterial puncture-site leakage. Remember: post-catheterization groin masses with turbulent color flow should raise concern for pseudoaneurysm.
vasculature-b5: The common iliac arteries normally should not exceed 2.0 cm in diameter; larger measurements suggest aneurysmal dilatation. Key fact: iliac aneurysms are often associated with abdominal aortic aneurysmal disease.
vasculature-b6: The inferior mesenteric artery supplies the distal large bowel, including the descending colon, sigmoid, and upper rectum. Memory aid: SMA supplies midgut; IMA supplies hindgut.
vasculature-b7: The left renal vein is longer because it must cross anterior to the aorta to reach the IVC on the right. Key fact: this longer course is why it can be compressed in nutcracker syndrome.
vasculature-b8: A true aneurysm involves dilation of all three vessel-wall layers: intima, media, and adventitia. Remember: 'true' means the actual vessel wall forms the aneurysm, unlike a pseudoaneurysm.
vasculature-b9: The left gastric artery is least likely to be seen sonographically because it is typically very small. Memory tip: the larger splenic vein, SMA, and proper hepatic artery are much more commonly identified on routine abdominal scans.
vasculature-b10: The image is normal, indicating expected vessel appearance and flow pattern without aneurysm, thrombus, or dissection. Key reminder: always compare caliber, wall contour, and Doppler flow to normal anatomic expectations.
vasculature-b11: The middle hepatic vein would not have hepatopetal flow because hepatic veins drain away from the liver into the IVC. Remember: hepatopetal means toward the liver, while portal venous flow is normally hepatopetal.
vasculature-b12: Nephroblastoma, also called Wilms tumor, is the pediatric renal tumor well known for extension into the renal vein and IVC. Memory fact: in children, a renal mass plus venous invasion strongly suggests Wilms tumor.
vasculature-b13: Nutcracker syndrome is compression of the left renal vein, usually between the SMA and aorta. Remember the name: the vein is being 'cracked' in the aortomesenteric angle.
vasculature-b14: A fusiform aneurysm is a symmetric, spindle-shaped dilation involving the full circumference of the vessel. Key fact: abdominal aortic aneurysms are most commonly fusiform rather than saccular.
vasculature-b15: A dissecting aneurysm is identified by an intimal tear creating a false lumen within the vessel wall. Memory tip: look for an intimal flap separating true and false lumens on imaging.
vasculature-b16: An intimal flap is the echogenic linear membrane seen within the aortic lumen, classic for dissection. Remember: a flap divides the vessel into true and false lumens.
vasculature-b17: IVC thrombosis appears as intraluminal echoes or filling defect within the inferior vena cava, which the arrow is indicating. Key fact: thrombus may make the IVC enlarged and less compressible.
vasculature-b18: The right gonadal vein drains directly into the IVC, while the left gonadal vein typically drains into the left renal vein. Memory tip: right goes straight, left takes the renal route.
vasculature-b19: The proper hepatic artery is the segment located within the liver hilum after the common hepatic artery gives off branches. Remember: 'proper' hepatic artery travels in the portal triad at the porta hepatis.
vasculature-b20: The splenic vein runs posterior to the pancreas and is a key landmark for outlining the posterior border of the pancreatic body and tail. Memory aid: the vein hugs the back of the pancreas.
vasculature-b21: In sagittal imaging, the right renal artery can appear as a circular anechoic vessel posterior to the IVC because it courses behind it toward the right kidney. Key fact: the right renal artery passes posterior to the IVC.
vasculature-b22: Marfan syndrome is a connective tissue disorder associated with tall stature and cardiovascular abnormalities including aortic root disease and mitral valve insufficiency. Remember: Marfan weakens elastic tissue, especially in the aorta.
vasculature-b23: The tunica intima is the innermost vessel layer and is directly in contact with flowing blood. Key fact: atherosclerotic plaque begins at the intimal layer.
vasculature-b24: The left renal vein normally courses between the SMA and the abdominal aorta in transverse imaging. Memory tip: this is the classic 'nutcracker' location of the left renal vein.
vasculature-b25: The celiac artery is the first main visceral branch arising from the abdominal aorta, just below the diaphragm. Remember the branch order: celiac first, then SMA, then renals.
vasculature-b26: An aneurysm caused by infection is called a mycotic aneurysm. Key fact: despite the name, 'mycotic' usually refers to infectious rather than specifically fungal origin.
vasculature-b27: This statement is the false one because the proximal abdominal aorta is actually deeper/more posterior, while the distal aorta becomes more anterior near the bifurcation. Remember: the spine and tapering abdomen make the distal aorta easier to see anteriorly.
vasculature-b28: The right gastric artery is not a primary branch of the celiac axis; the classic celiac branches are left gastric, splenic, and common hepatic. Memory aid: think 'L-S-H' for the celiac trifurcation.
vasculature-b29: The tunica adventitia is the outermost vessel wall layer, providing support and anchoring the vessel to surrounding tissues. Remember: adventitia = exterior covering.
vasculature-b30: After a meal, the SMA supplies the active bowel and therefore demonstrates low-resistance flow with increased diastolic component. Key fact: fasting SMA is higher resistance, postprandial SMA becomes low resistance.
vasculature-b31: The SMA is the second unpaired anterior branch of the abdominal aorta, arising just inferior to the celiac trunk. Remember: celiac first, SMA second, IMA third.
vasculature-b32: The SMA normally changes from high resistance when fasting to low resistance after a meal because intestinal demand increases. Key memory fact: postprandial bowel needs more blood flow, so SMA diastolic flow rises.
vasculature-b33: A fasting SMA normally demonstrates a high-resistance waveform because the small bowel has lower metabolic demand between meals. Remember: fasting gut equals less continuous forward diastolic flow.
vasculature-b34: In small bowel ischemia, the postprandial SMA may remain high resistance instead of converting to low resistance. Key fact: failure of the SMA to increase diastolic flow after eating suggests compromised bowel perfusion.
vasculature-b35: An abdominal aortic aneurysm is defined when the abdominal aorta measures greater than 3 cm in diameter. Remember: 3 cm is the classic AAA cutoff used in ultrasound.
vasculature-b36: Budd–Chiari syndrome refers to hepatic venous outflow obstruction, typically involving the hepatic veins. Memory tip: think 'Budd' equals blocked drainage from the liver.
vasculature-b37: Most abdominal aortic aneurysms are fusiform, meaning they involve a circumferential widening of the vessel. Key fact: fusiform is far more common than the more focal saccular type.
vasculature-b38: The celiac artery and its major branches create the classic 'seagull sign' on transverse imaging. Remember: the celiac trunk is short, then quickly divides into wing-like branches.
vasculature-b39: The splenic artery can mimic the main pancreatic duct because it courses along the superior posterior pancreas and may appear tubular on sonography. Key fact: color Doppler helps distinguish vessel from duct.
vasculature-b40: The IVC carries systemic venous blood back to the heart and terminates in the right atrium. Memory tip: veins return to the atria, and the IVC specifically drains into the right side.
vasculature-b41: A persistently high-resistive SMA waveform during vascular evaluation suggests small bowel ischemia because normal demand-related diastolic flow is not achieved. Key fact: ischemic bowel often prevents the expected low-resistance postprandial pattern.
vasculature-b42: The main portal vein is formed by the confluence of the splenic vein and superior mesenteric vein. Remember: SMV + splenic vein behind the pancreas forms the portal vein.
vasculature-b43: The hepatic veins drain directly into the IVC just below the diaphragm. Key memory fact: on longitudinal imaging, they often appear to fan into the IVC near the liver dome.
vasculature-b44: The aorta originates from the left ventricle, which pumps oxygenated blood into systemic circulation. Remember: left ventricle to aorta, right ventricle to pulmonary artery.
vasculature-b45: The IVC is commonly divided into hepatic, prerenal, renal, and postrenal segments; 'pancreatic' is not one of its sections. Key fact: segment names are based on nearby major organs or vessels, not the pancreas.
vasculature-b46: The hepatic artery supplies the liver continuously, so it normally shows low-resistance arterial flow with forward diastolic flow. Remember: organs with constant metabolic demand, like the liver and kidneys, have low-resistance waveforms.
vasculature-b47: AAA commonly causes back pain, abdominal bruit, and lower-extremity pain from emboli or poor distal perfusion, but not elevated hematocrit. Key memory: rupture or blood loss would more likely lower hematocrit, not raise it.
vasculature-b48: An echogenic linear structure gently swaying within the aortic lumen is classic for an intimal flap, indicating aortic dissection. Remember: dissection creates true and false lumens separated by a mobile flap.
vasculature-b49: The left gonadal vein drains into the left renal vein, whereas the right gonadal vein drains directly into the IVC. Memory tip: the left side often takes the 'renal vein route.'
vasculature-b50: The common iliac artery supplies the lower extremities, a vascular bed that normally has high peripheral resistance, producing a high-resistance waveform. Remember: extremity arteries at rest are typically triphasic and high resistance.
vasculature-b51: The inferior mesenteric vein often joins the splenic vein before the portal confluence forms. Key fact: the portal vein is usually formed by the union of the splenic vein and superior mesenteric vein.
vasculature-b52: The left renal vein crosses anterior to the aorta and therefore lies directly anterior to the left renal artery. Remember the classic relationship: vein anterior, artery posterior.
vasculature-b53: If an EVAR does not fully exclude the aneurysm sac from blood flow, persistent sac perfusion is called an endoleak. Memory tip: 'endo-' means blood is still leaking inside the repaired aneurysm sac.
vasculature-b54: A linear echo within the aortic lumen with flow on both sides is an intimal flap, the hallmark of aortic dissection. Key fact: Marfan syndrome predisposes patients to dissection because of weakened connective tissue.
vasculature-b55: The right renal vein is the shortest because the IVC lies on the right side of the spine, very close to the right kidney. Remember: right vein short, left vein long.
vasculature-b56: Right-sided heart failure elevates central venous pressure, causing dilation of the IVC and hepatic veins. Memory aid: when the right heart backs up, the venous system behind it enlarges.
vasculature-b57: Hepatic veins normally demonstrate a pulsatile, often triphasic waveform because they are influenced directly by right atrial and cardiac pressure changes. Remember: hepatic veins reflect the heartbeat more than most abdominal veins.
vasculature-b58: The IVC normally should not exceed about 2.5 cm in diameter. Key fact: a dilated IVC can suggest elevated right atrial pressure or right-sided heart dysfunction.
vasculature-b59: The false statement is that the IVC is to the left of the aorta; normally, the IVC lies to the right of the abdominal aorta. Remember: 'IVC = right-sided companion' to the aorta.
vasculature-b60: This statement is false because most abdominal aortic aneurysms are true aneurysms, involving all three vessel wall layers. Key fact: the most common AAA location is infrarenal, below the renal arteries.
gi-b1: In hypertrophic pyloric stenosis, the pyloric muscle thickness should not exceed 3 mm. Remember: the classic ultrasound cutoff is muscle thickness >3 mm, with channel elongation often supporting the diagnosis.
gi-b2: Hypertrophic pyloric stenosis most commonly presents at 2 to 6 weeks of age. A helpful memory clue is that affected infants are typically young newborns who develop progressive nonbilious projectile vomiting after feeding.
gi-b3: The cervix sign describes the elongated, narrowed pyloric canal in longitudinal view, resembling the uterine cervix. Think longitudinal pylorus equals cervix sign, while transverse views more often produce target-type appearances.
gi-b4: Weight gain is least likely because hypertrophic pyloric stenosis causes persistent vomiting, leading instead to poor weight gain or weight loss. Classic associated findings include projectile vomiting, dehydration, and a palpable olive.
gi-b5: A normal appendix should measure no more than 6 mm in anteroposterior diameter. The key rule to remember is: noncompressible blind-ending tubular structure over 6 mm suggests appendicitis.
gi-b6: Leukocytosis is a common accompanying finding in acute appendicitis because it reflects the inflammatory response. Pair RLQ pain, nausea, and an elevated white blood cell count as a classic appendicitis triad.
gi-b7: The thyroid in the belly sign refers to hyperechoic edematous connective tissue surrounding an inflamed appendix. It looks bright from inflamed periappendiceal fat, a useful secondary sign of appendicitis on ultrasound.
gi-b8: The large white arrow indicates the stomach. On upper abdominal sonography, recognizing the stomach helps orient adjacent structures like the pylorus and transverse colon.
gi-b9: The right colic flexure is also called the hepatic flexure because it lies adjacent to the liver. Easy memory aid: right side equals hepatic, left side equals splenic flexure.
gi-b10: Volvulus is the term for twisting of the bowel, which can compromise both obstruction and blood flow. Remember: volvulus = twist, intussusception = telescoping.
gi-b11: Paraumbilical hernia is the most common type of ventral hernia. A memory tip is that ventral hernias frequently occur along the anterior abdominal wall near the umbilicus.
gi-b12: The most common abdominal wall location for endometriosis is a Cesarean section scar. Think scar implantation: ectopic endometrial tissue is often seeded in prior pelvic or uterine surgical incisions.
gi-b13: Melanoma is a commonly encountered source of bowel metastases because it has a strong tendency for widespread hematogenous spread, including to the GI tract. Remember: melanoma loves to metastasize almost anywhere.
gi-b14: Diverticulitis most often affects the sigmoid colon and is therefore most commonly found in the left lower quadrant. The key association is LLQ pain in an older patient with sigmoid diverticular disease.
gi-b15: Rectus sheath hematoma may occur during defecation because straining can tear epigastric vessels or muscle fibers. Remember that coughing, exertion, and anticoagulation are other classic precipitating factors.
gi-b31: Cyclical pain is classic for scar endometriosis because ectopic endometrial tissue in a cesarean scar responds to monthly hormonal changes. Memory tip: pain that flares with menses strongly suggests endometriosis.
gi-b32: Red currant jelly stools are classically associated with intussusception due to mucus mixed with blood from bowel ischemia. Memory tip: telescoping bowel can produce the hallmark "jelly" stool.
gi-b33: Intussusception is the exception because it usually presents differently from pyloric stenosis, with episodic pain and sometimes currant jelly stools rather than isolated gastric outlet obstruction. Memory tip: pyloric stenosis mimics involve vomiting disorders, not telescoping bowel.
gi-b34: Watery diarrhea is a common clinical feature of colitis because inflammation of the colon disrupts normal fluid absorption. Memory tip: colon inflammation often leads to frequent loose stools.
gi-b35: Most gastric cancers are adenocarcinomas because they arise from the glandular mucosa lining the stomach. Memory tip: stomach cancer usually comes from the gastric glands, so think adenocarcinoma.
gi-b36: A hair-filled obstructing mass is called a trichobezoar; "tricho" means hair. Memory tip: trichobezoar = hair bezoar, while phyto- refers to plant material.
gi-b37: Crohn disease is an autoimmune inflammatory bowel disease marked by recurrent episodes of GI tract inflammation. Memory tip: Crohn can affect any part of the GI tract, often in a patchy pattern.
gi-b38: Intussusception is the telescoping of one bowel segment into another, often causing obstruction. Memory tip: think of one section sliding inside the next like a collapsible telescope.
gi-b39: A mechanical obstruction means the bowel is physically blocked by a mass, adhesion, hernia, or similar lesion. Memory tip: mechanical = something is actually in the way.
gi-b40: Valsalva is useful because raising intra-abdominal pressure can provoke or accentuate a hernia during scanning. Memory tip: if the hernia hides at rest, have the patient strain.
gi-b41: An inguinal hernia is bowel protruding into the groin through the inguinal region. Memory tip: inguinal = groin.
gi-b42: A spigelian hernia occurs through a weakened area of the lower abdominal wall near the semilunar line, often in the lower rectus region. Memory tip: spigelian hernias are lateral ventral hernias.
gi-b43: McBurney point is the classic site of maximal pain and rebound tenderness in acute appendicitis. Memory tip: appendicitis pain localizes to McBurney point in the right lower quadrant.
gi-b44: McBurney point lies halfway between the anterior superior iliac spine and the umbilicus, the classic surface landmark for appendicitis. Memory tip: ASIS to umbilicus, then find the midpoint.
gi-b45: The olive sign is an enlarged palpable pyloric sphincter felt in hypertrophic pyloric stenosis. Memory tip: the firm pylorus feels like a small olive in the epigastrium or RUQ.
gi-b46: Rebound tenderness suggests peritoneal irritation and is a classic clinical sign of acute appendicitis. Remember: pain that worsens when pressure is released is more concerning for an inflamed appendix than simple bowel upset.
gi-b47: The vermiform appendix most commonly arises from the cecum, near the ileocecal region in the right lower quadrant. Key memory fact: the appendix is a blind-ending tube attached to the cecal base.
gi-b48: Diverticulosis is the presence of small mucosal outpouchings, most often in the sigmoid colon. Remember: “-osis” means the diverticula are present; “-itis” means they are inflamed.
gi-b49: A rectus sheath hematoma is a bleed, so hematocrit typically decreases rather than increases. A helpful clue is that coughing, sneezing, trauma, or childbirth can precipitate abdominal wall bleeding.
gi-b50: Crohn disease typically shows bowel wall thickening, hyperemia, and often a noncompressible target appearance, not increased peristalsis. Remember: inflamed bowel in Crohn disease is more often stiff and hypoactive than overactive.
gi-b51: Vomiting, red currant jelly stools, and leukocytosis can occur with intussusception, but being a first-born male infant is not a typical clinical finding. Memory tip: think obstruction symptoms plus bloody mucus stool.
gi-b52: Fluid-filled, distended bowel loops are a classic sonographic sign of intestinal obstruction because contents cannot pass normally. Key fact: obstructed bowel often appears dilated proximal to the blockage.
gi-b53: Intussusception has traditionally been treated with a therapeutic enema, which can both diagnose and reduce the telescoped bowel. Remember: air or contrast enema is often first-line nonoperative management.
gi-b54: Intussusception is the most common cause of intestinal obstruction in children younger than 2 years. Memory aid: in infants and toddlers, telescoping bowel is a leading emergency cause of obstruction.
gi-b55: Sonographically seeing fluid and gas bubbles move retrograde from the stomach into the esophagus indicates gastroesophageal reflux disease. Key fact: reflux is demonstrated by backward flow across the gastroesophageal junction.
gi-b56: The infant is often placed in the right lateral decubitus position to improve visualization of the pyloric sphincter. Remember: this position helps fluid fill the antrum and outlines the pylorus better.
gi-b57: Left lower quadrant pain with fever and alternating constipation and diarrhea is a classic presentation of diverticulitis, usually involving the sigmoid colon. Memory tip: sigmoid disease commonly causes LLQ pain in adults.
gi-b58: Pyloric stenosis is diagnosed when the pyloric muscle measures about 3 mm or more in thickness and 17 mm or more in length. Remember the classic cutoff pair: 3 mm thick, 17 mm long.
gi-b59: Crohn disease commonly causes abdominal pain, rectal bleeding, and weight loss, but a palpable abdominal mass is not a typical clinical finding. Key fact: Crohn is an inflammatory bowel disease with chronic GI symptoms and malnutrition risk.
gi-b60: Antibiotic therapy can disrupt normal bowel flora and lead to colitis, including pseudomembranous colitis. Remember: recent antibiotic use is a classic history clue when evaluating inflammatory colonic symptoms.
gi-b16: Phytobezoars, composed of indigestible plant material, are most common in older adults and can obstruct the small bowel. Remember: “phyto” means plant, making this bezoar type the classic food-fiber obstruction.
gi-b17: Intussusception typically appears as a bowel mass with an outer diameter greater than 3 cm on ultrasound. A useful memory aid is that the target or doughnut sign is larger than normal bowel loops.
gi-b18: In an 18-month-old with intermittent severe pain and vomiting, a right lower quadrant target-like mass is most consistent with intussusception. Remember the classic pediatric triad: episodic pain, vomiting, and a bowel-within-bowel ultrasound appearance.
gi-b19: An appendicolith is a calcified deposit within the appendix and appears as an echogenic focus, often with posterior shadowing. It is a key sonographic clue that supports acute appendicitis in the right lower quadrant.
gi-b20: The superficial mucosa is one of the echogenic layers of the bowel wall on sonography. To remember the alternating pattern, bowel wall layers typically alternate bright-dark-bright-dark-bright from lumen outward.
gi-b21: Midgut malrotation is suggested when the normal SMA-SMV relationship is reversed, with the SMA lying to the right of the SMV. In bilious vomiting, this vascular malposition is a critical red flag for malrotation.
gi-b22: The gastroesophageal junction can be seen in sagittal imaging as a bull’seye structure anterior to the aorta and posterior to the left lobe of the liver. This landmark helps identify the distal esophagus entering the stomach.
gi-b23: Visceral is not one of the standard sonographic bowel wall layers; the recognized layers include mucosa, submucosa, muscularis, and serosa. Remember: ultrasound bowel wall anatomy is described by histologic wall layers, not the term “visceral.”
gi-b24: Normal bowel is usually compressible, so the statement that it does not compress is the exception. A quick rule: normal bowel generally shows peristalsis, low Doppler flow, and yields under graded compression.
gi-b25: A shadowing echogenic focus within a hyperemic blind-ended tubular structure in the right lower quadrant is most likely an appendicolith. This finding strongly supports appendicitis because the blind-ended tube is the inflamed appendix.
gi-b26: In pyloric stenosis, the pyloric muscle is thickened, not focally thinned, making that choice the exception. Remember the classic ultrasound features: elongated pylorus, doughnut sign in transverse, and cervix sign in longitudinal view.
gi-b27: An inflamed appendix is classically noncompressible, so a compressible blind-ended tube is not typical of acute appendicitis. Key appendicitis signs include appendicolith, hyperemia, and possible periappendiceal fluid.
gi-b28: Constipation is not a classic clinical feature of acute appendicitis. More typical findings are right lower quadrant pain, rebound tenderness, and leukocytosis, reflecting localized inflammation and irritation.
gi-b29: Pyloric stenosis classically occurs in first-born males, not first-born females, making that the exception. Remember the typical infant presentation: progressive nonbilious vomiting, dehydration, weight loss, and sometimes a palpable olive.
gi-b30: Pseudomyxoma peritonei commonly results from mucin-producing appendiceal neoplasms that seed the peritoneum. A key memory fact is “jelly belly” from mucinous appendix cancer spreading throughout the abdomen.
chest-b16: Lung consolidation is the replacement of normal air in alveoli by fluid, pus, blood, or tumor cells, making the lung more tissue-like. Remember: consolidated lung becomes "solid" instead of air-filled.
chest-b17: The right lung has three lobes: upper, middle, and lower, separated by the horizontal and oblique fissures. Memory aid: right = 3 lobes, left = 2 lobes because the heart takes space on the left.
chest-b18: A pneumothorax is free air in the pleural space outside the lung, which can partially or completely collapse the lung. Remember: "pneumo" = air and "thorax" = chest.
chest-b19: Pulmonary sequestration is nonfunctioning lung tissue that is separate from the normal bronchial tree and has its own systemic blood supply. Key fact: it often receives blood from the aorta, not the pulmonary artery.
chest-b20: The thymus is responsible for producing and maturing T lymphocytes in children. Remember: the "T" in thymus helps you recall T cells.
chest-b21: Congenital cystic adenomatoid malformation is a fetal chest mass made of abnormal bronchial and pulmonary tissue. Key fact: it is now often called congenital pulmonary airway malformation (CPAM).
chest-b22: Thoracentesis is the procedure used to remove fluid from the pleural space for diagnosis or treatment. Memory aid: "thoraco-" refers to the chest, while "-centesis" means puncture.
chest-b23: Pericardial effusion is fluid within the pericardial sac surrounding the heart, so arrows around the heart typically indicate this collection. Remember: peri- means around, and cardial refers to the heart.
chest-b24: Pneumothorax is a known complication of thoracentesis because air can accidentally enter the pleural space during the procedure. Key fact: post-procedure chest imaging is often used to check for it.
chest-b25: A hematoma can appear hyperechoic, hypoechoic, or complex depending on its age and stage of clot organization. Remember: blood changes appearance over time, so hematomas are variable.
chest-b26: A chest radiograph is the typical first test used to diagnose pneumothorax by showing pleural air and possible lung collapse. Key fact: an upright chest x-ray often best demonstrates free pleural air.
chest-b27: A pleural effusion associated with pneumonia is called a parapneumonic effusion. Remember: "para-" means alongside, so it occurs alongside pneumonia.
chest-b28: Fluid around the heart is called a pericardial effusion because it collects in the pericardial sac. Memory aid: peri- = around, cardial = heart.
chest-b29: In pediatric patients, the thymus commonly appears as an echogenic mass with linear and punctate echogenicities. Key fact: this gives the classic "starry sky" appearance.
chest-b30: Retroperitoneal fibrosis most commonly appears as a hypoechoic mass surrounding the aorta in the retroperitoneum. Remember: it often encases retroperitoneal vessels and may obstruct the ureters.
chest-b1: Pleural effusion is fluid in the pleural space, so on abdominal/chest sonography it appears as an anechoic collection superior to the diaphragm. Remember: fluid above the diaphragm suggests pleural effusion; below it suggests ascites.
chest-b2: The psoas muscle lies immediately adjacent to the lumbar vertebral bodies, making it the muscle closest to the spine. Memory tip: psoas originates from the lumbar spine itself.
chest-b3: A transudate effusion results from altered hydrostatic or oncotic pressures, such as in CHF or hypoalbuminemia, rather than inflammation. Think: transudate = pressure problem, exudate = inflammatory problem.
chest-b4: Migraine medication use is a recognized clinical association with retroperitoneal fibrosis, especially older ergot-derived drugs. Key fact: retroperitoneal fibrosis can be idiopathic or drug-related and often causes ureteral obstruction.
chest-b5: Exudate effusions are linked to inflammation, infection, or malignancy because they contain protein-rich fluid leaking from inflamed pleura. Remember: exudate = inflammatory, transudate = pressure imbalance.
chest-b6: An anechoic fluid collection superior to the diaphragm is most consistent with pleural effusion, meaning fluid around the lung. Key fact: pleural fluid often layers dependently above the diaphragm on ultrasound.
chest-b7: Empyema is a pleural effusion that contains pus, usually from infection in the pleural space. Memory aid: 'pyo-' means pus, and empyema is infected pleural fluid.
chest-b8: The sandwich sign describes mesenteric vessels and fat encased by enlarged lymph nodes, a classic appearance of abdominal lymphadenopathy. Remember: nodes form the 'bread' around central vessels.
chest-b9: Lymph nodes measuring more than 10 mm are generally considered abnormal in many abdominal imaging contexts. Key fact: enlarged nodes raise concern for infection, inflammation, or malignancy.
chest-b10: The thymus is located in the mediastinum, specifically the anterior superior mediastinum. Memory tip: the thymus sits behind the sternum and is prominent in children.
chest-b11: Fluid around the lungs is called a pleural effusion because it collects in the pleural space. Remember: pleural = around the lungs; pericardial = around the heart.
chest-b12: The seashore sign on M-mode represents normal lung sliding, with a granular pattern below the pleural line. Memory aid: normal sliding looks like waves meeting sand at the beach.
chest-b13: In hemophiliac patients, the psoas muscle is the most common site of retroperitoneal hematoma because it is deep and highly vascular. Key fact: psoas bleeding can cause flank pain and limited hip motion.
chest-b14: The lungs are not within the mediastinum; they lie lateral to it in the pleural cavities. Remember: the mediastinum is the central thoracic compartment between the lungs.
chest-b15: The left lung has two lobes, upper and lower, to accommodate the space taken by the heart. Memory tip: left lung = 2 lobes, right lung = 3 lobes.
chest-b31: Fluid seen adjacent to the heart in the midline subxiphoid view is most consistent with a pericardial effusion, not pleural or peritoneal fluid. Remember: pericardial fluid outlines the heart within the pericardial sac.
chest-b32: The quadratus lumborum lies posterior and lateral to the kidney in the retroperitoneum. A good memory aid is “QL = back wall beside the kidney.”
chest-b33: Retroperitoneal fibrosis commonly encases retroperitoneal structures like the aorta and IVC, but the rectum is a pelvic bowel structure and is not typically involved. Think: this disease wraps retroperitoneal vessels, not intraperitoneal bowel.
chest-b34: Retroperitoneal hematoma is typically associated with bleeding, so trauma, hemophilia, and low hematocrit fit; weight loss does not. Remember: hematoma presents with acute blood-loss findings rather than chronic constitutional symptoms.
chest-b35: Enlargement of abdominal lymph nodes is called retroperitoneal lymphadenopathy. The suffix “-pathy” refers to disease or abnormality, and enlarged nodes along the aorta are a classic example.
chest-b36: The crus of the diaphragm is a linear muscular extension that attaches to the upper lumbar vertebrae. Key fact: the crura are diaphragmatic muscle fibers seen adjacent to the aorta in the upper retroperitoneum.
chest-b37: Pneumonia, hemorrhage, and carcinoma can all produce lung consolidation, but pulmonary sequestration is a congenital lung anomaly rather than a typical cause of consolidation. Remember: consolidation usually means alveoli are filled with fluid, pus, blood, or tumor.
chest-b38: A pneumothorax is a known complication of thoracentesis and may require chest radiography for confirmation. Key fact: introducing air into the pleural space can cause partial lung collapse.
chest-b39: Abdominal lymph nodes are commonly found in the mesentery, renal hilum, and along the aorta, but not typically within the subhepatic space. Think of abdominal nodes tracking with major vessels and mesentery.
chest-b40: Lung consolidation often shows branching linear internal echoes from air within bronchi, known as air bronchograms. Memory tip: consolidated lung can appear “liver-like” with bright branching lines.
chest-b41: Multiple hypoechoic masses along the anterior border of the abdominal aorta are classic for retroperitoneal lymphadenopathy. Remember: enlarged para-aortic nodes often appear as clustered masses in this location.
chest-b42: Thoracentesis is typically performed with the patient upright to allow pleural fluid to collect dependently for safer access. Key fact: sitting up helps the fluid layer out posteriorly and inferiorly.
chest-b43: A large hypoechoic abdominal mass in a patient with weight loss, malaise, and migraine medication use is most suggestive of retroperitoneal fibrosis. Remember: some drugs are associated with this fibrotic process encasing retroperitoneal structures.
chest-b44: Abnormal lymph nodes usually enlarge, often lose the echogenic hilum, and may be associated with infection or malignancy; therefore, they do not tend to measure less than 1 cm. Key fact: increasing size is a major warning sign for pathologic nodes.
chest-b45: Pleural effusion commonly accompanies lung consolidation, especially with pneumonia or other inflammatory processes. Remember: fluid in the pleural space often provides an acoustic window to visualize consolidated lung.
chest-b46: A heterogeneous fluid collection above the right hemidiaphragm in a patient with dyspnea is most consistent with a complex pleural effusion. Remember: pleural fluid lies superior to the diaphragm, while liver/gallbladder pathology is below it.
chest-b47: Hematocrit helps assess for active bleeding because it reflects the proportion of red blood cells in blood and may fall with hemorrhage. After a femoral puncture, declining Hct can support suspicion for retroperitoneal bleeding.
chest-b48: Infected pleural effusions commonly contain debris, fibrin, or loculations, so they usually appear complex on ultrasound. Key memory aid: infection makes simple fluid look 'dirty' rather than purely anechoic.
chest-b49: Hemophilia is an inherited bleeding disorder caused by deficiency of clotting factors, impairing normal blood coagulation. Remember: hemophiliacs do not have a red cell problem—they have a clotting problem.
chest-b50: Consolidated lung often becomes 'hepatized,' meaning it can look isoechoic to the liver on ultrasound. This liver-like appearance is a classic clue to lung consolidation adjacent to the pleura.
chest-b51: Abnormal enlarged lymph nodes often lose their normal echogenic hilum and become more anechoic or hypoechoic. A helpful clue is that diseased nodes usually look darker than normal nodes.
chest-b52: Bronchial infections are generally not well evaluated sonographically because air-filled lung blocks ultrasound transmission. In contrast, pleural effusions, lymphomas, and thymomas may be detected when they abut accessible soft tissues.
chest-b53: The transversalis fascia lies between the transversus abdominis muscle and the peritoneum, lining the anterolateral abdominal wall. Remember: it is the deep fascial layer just superficial to the peritoneum.
chest-b54: The visceral pleura directly covers and adheres to the lung surface. Memory tip: 'visceral' refers to the organ itself, so visceral pleura stays with the lung.
chest-b55: The parietal pleura lines the inner chest wall rather than the lung surface. Remember: 'parietal' means wall, so parietal pleura is the pleural lining of the thoracic cavity.
chest-b56: A therapeutic thoracentesis is performed to remove excess pleural fluid and relieve symptoms such as shortness of breath. Key distinction: therapeutic = treatment, whereas diagnostic = sampling to determine cause.
chest-b57: In adults, the thymus usually involutes and is typically not seen sonographically. Remember: the thymus is prominent in infants and children but regresses after puberty.
chest-b58: The right portal vein is not retroperitoneal because it is located within the liver in the intraperitoneal upper abdomen. By contrast, the aorta and IVC are classic retroperitoneal vessels.
chest-b59: The mesentery is a double fold of peritoneum that suspends the intestines from the posterior abdominal wall. A useful memory fact: it also carries vessels, lymphatics, and nerves to the bowel.
chest-b60: Diagnostic thoracentesis is used to obtain pleural fluid for analysis and determine its origin or cause. Remember: if the question asks why the fluid is there, think diagnostic thoracentesis.
neck-b1: A cystic hygroma is another name for a lymphangioma, a congenital malformation of the lymphatic system. Remember: hygromas are classically multiloculated cystic neck masses in infants and children.
neck-b2: Exophthalmos means anterior protrusion or bulging of the eyeballs, a classic finding in thyroid eye disease. Remember: Graves disease is the board favorite association with exophthalmos.
neck-b3: Graves disease can be associated with menstrual irregularities, including oligomenorrhea, because hyperthyroidism affects normal reproductive hormone balance. Remember: hyperthyroid symptoms often extend beyond the neck to systemic and menstrual changes.
neck-b4: Pretibial myxedema is a classic extrathyroidal manifestation of Graves disease caused by autoimmune dermal infiltration. Remember the Graves triad: hyperthyroidism, exophthalmos, and pretibial myxedema.
neck-b5: Dysphagia specifically means difficulty swallowing, often reported with esophageal or compressive neck pathology. Remember: "-phagia" relates to eating or swallowing, while "dys-" means impaired.
neck-b6: Weight gain, menorrhagia, and cold intolerance are classic hypothyroid symptoms, making autoimmune lymphocytic thyroiditis the best answer. Remember: Hashimoto-type thyroiditis commonly causes an underactive thyroid state.
neck-b7: The measured mid-neck structure should not exceed 10 mm, which is the usual upper limit used for this normal anatomic measurement. Remember: 10 mm is a common cutoff when assessing neck soft-tissue dimensions on ultrasound.
neck-b8: The red asterisk marks the common carotid artery, a round, pulsatile vessel typically seen medial to the internal jugular vein. Remember: on transverse neck imaging, the CCA is usually smaller and less compressible than the IJV.
neck-b9: The blue asterisk indicates the internal jugular vein, which lies lateral to the common carotid artery and is easily compressible. Remember: veins are usually larger, more variable in shape, and compress with probe pressure.
neck-b10: The orange asterisk identifies the right sternocleidomastoid muscle, a key superficial landmark in transverse neck imaging. Remember: the SCM overlies the carotid sheath structures in the lateral neck.
neck-b11: In a patient with prior papillary thyroid carcinoma, abnormal lateral neck structures are most suspicious for metastatic disease in lymph nodes. Remember: papillary thyroid cancer commonly spreads first to cervical lymph nodes.
neck-b12: Internal microcalcifications are worrisome because punctate echogenic foci within a thyroid nodule strongly suggest malignancy, especially papillary carcinoma. Remember: microcalcifications are one of the highest-risk thyroid nodule features.
neck-b13: A colloid cyst typically shows benign cystic features and may demonstrate comet-tail artifact from colloid crystals. Remember: comet-tail artifact in a thyroid cyst strongly favors a benign colloid lesion.
neck-b14: Thyroid volume is calculated as length × width × thickness × 0.529, which approximates the volume of an ellipsoid. Remember: each thyroid lobe is measured separately, then the lobar volumes are added.
neck-b15: The lesion most likely represents a benign thyroid nodule based on its imaging appearance rather than aggressive malignant features. Remember: many thyroid nodules are benign, especially when they lack microcalcifications, irregular margins, or marked hypoechogenicity.
neck-b16: Hypercalcemia is least likely with goiter because goiter commonly causes compressive symptoms like dysphagia, dyspnea, and hoarseness, not elevated calcium. Remember: hypercalcemia points more toward parathyroid disease than thyroid enlargement.
neck-b17: Amylase is the digestive enzyme found in saliva and begins carbohydrate digestion in the mouth. Remember: salivary amylase starts breaking down starch before food even reaches the stomach.
neck-b18: The main duct of the parotid gland is Stenson duct, which carries saliva into the oral cavity near the upper molars. Remember: parotid = Stenson, while submandibular = Wharton.
neck-b19: Graves disease is also called diffuse toxic goiter because it causes diffuse thyroid enlargement with hyperthyroidism. Remember: Graves is the classic cause of a hypervascular, overactive diffuse goiter.
neck-b20: The internal jugular vein is the most lateral vascular structure adjacent to the thyroid on a transverse neck scan. Remember: the carotid artery lies more medial, and the jugular vein sits lateral to it.
neck-b21: Hypercalcemia should raise suspicion for a parathyroid adenoma because excess parathyroid hormone increases serum calcium. Remember: high calcium in the neck workup often means 'look at the parathyroids.'
neck-b22: Thyroglossal duct cysts are benign congenital cysts typically found in the midline near the hyoid bone, superior to the thyroid. Remember: they arise along the embryologic descent path of the thyroid.
neck-b23: The normal adult neck usually contains four parathyroid glands, typically two superior and two inferior. Remember: '4 parathyroids' is the classic anatomy, though location can vary.
neck-b24: A branchial cleft cyst commonly appears as a cystic mass near the mandibular angle along the lateral neck. Remember: branchial cleft cysts are lateral, while thyroglossal duct cysts are usually midline.
neck-b25: A cold nodule is more likely to be malignant because it is nonfunctioning on nuclear medicine imaging. Remember: hot nodules usually produce hormone and are more often benign.
neck-b26: The parathyroid glands regulate calcium through parathyroid hormone, which affects bone, kidneys, and intestines. Remember: parathyroids = calcium control, not thyroid hormone production.
neck-b27: A normal cervical lymph node generally should not measure greater than 10 mm in short-axis size. Remember: benign nodes are usually small, oval, and maintain an echogenic hilum.
neck-b28: Elevated serum calcium is associated with parathyroid adenoma because excess PTH increases calcium levels in the blood. Remember: parathyroid adenoma is a classic cause of primary hyperparathyroidism.
neck-b29: A normal cervical lymph node is typically hypoechoic and oblong with a distinct echogenic hilum, reflecting preserved benign architecture. Remember: oval shape plus fatty hilum strongly suggests a normal/reactive node.
neck-b30: A thyroid inferno describes markedly increased diffuse thyroid vascularity, which is characteristic of Graves disease. Remember: color Doppler 'inferno' is a classic imaging clue for Graves.
neck-b31: Hyperechogenicity is more typical of a benign thyroid nodule, whereas malignant nodules more often appear hypoechoic and may show microcalcifications, nodal spread, or be solitary. Memory tip: “dark and tiny bright specks” can suggest cancer.
neck-b32: A “cold” nodule is a nuclear medicine finding for reduced tracer uptake and is not a benign diagnostic sonographic feature. Remember: simple anechoic cysts, eggshell calcification, and hyperechogenicity more often favor benignity.
neck-b33: Papillary carcinoma is the most common thyroid cancer by far and often spreads to cervical lymph nodes. Key fact: despite nodal metastases, papillary thyroid cancer generally has an excellent prognosis.
neck-b34: Hashimoto thyroiditis is the most common cause of hypothyroidism because autoimmune destruction of the gland lowers hormone production. Memory tip: Hashimoto = chronic lymphocytic thyroiditis leading to an underactive thyroid.
neck-b35: An echogenic hilum is usually a normal or benign lymph node feature, while abnormal nodes tend to be enlarged, round, or contain calcifications. Remember: loss of the fatty hilum raises concern for pathology.
neck-b36: Graves disease is the most common cause of hyperthyroidism due to autoimmune stimulation of the thyroid. Key sonographic fact: it often causes a diffusely enlarged, hypervascular gland—“thyroid inferno.”
neck-b37: The parotid gland lies immediately anterior and inferior to the ear, making it the salivary gland in that location. Memory tip: parotid pathology often presents near the preauricular region.
neck-b38: Fibromatosis colli most commonly involves the sternocleidomastoid muscle and is a classic cause of infant torticollis. Remember: a firm SCM mass in a newborn strongly suggests this diagnosis.
neck-b39: Graves disease best fits hyperthyroid symptoms with exophthalmos, a hallmark extrathyroidal finding. Memory tip: weight loss + hyperthyroidism + bulging eyes points strongly to Graves.
neck-b40: Colloid is the thyroid follicular fluid that stores thyroid hormone precursors within the gland. Key fact: on ultrasound, colloid can create comet-tail artifact in benign colloid nodules.
neck-b41: Hashimoto thyroiditis commonly results in too few thyroid hormones because autoimmune damage impairs normal gland function. Remember: Hashimoto is the classic cause of primary hypothyroidism.
neck-b42: After thyroidectomy for papillary carcinoma, a new palpable neck mass is most likely metastatic or reactive lymphadenopathy. Key fact: papillary thyroid cancer commonly spreads first to cervical lymph nodes.
neck-b43: Wharton duct is the excretory duct of the submandibular gland and opens at the floor of the mouth. Memory tip: Stensen duct belongs to the parotid gland, not the submandibular gland.
neck-b44: The thyroid requires iodine to synthesize T3 and T4 hormones. Remember: without adequate iodine, the gland cannot make normal thyroid hormone and may enlarge into a goiter.
neck-b45: The longus colli muscles lie posterior to each thyroid lobe and are an important landmark on thyroid ultrasound. Memory tip: strap muscles are anterior; longus colli is posterior.
neck-b46: The sternocleidomastoid muscles lie lateral and somewhat anterior to each thyroid lobe on neck ultrasound. Remember: strap muscles are anterior, longus colli is posterior, and SCM forms the lateral muscular landmark.
neck-b47: Fibromatosis colli is a benign enlargement/fibrosis of the sternocleidomastoid muscle and is classically linked to congenital muscular torticollis. Key memory tip: torticollis in infants often points to the SCM.
neck-b48: The esophagus can mimic a posterior left thyroid or parathyroid mass because it sits just posterior to the left thyroid lobe near the trachea. Remember: it often shows a layered wall and may contain air or moving contents.
neck-b49: The common carotid artery lies immediately lateral to each thyroid lobe and is the closest major vascular landmark. A helpful memory aid is the classic thyroid transverse view: gland medial, carotid lateral, jugular more lateral/superficial.
neck-b50: An isthmus thicker than 10 mm suggests thyroid enlargement. Remember that the normal isthmus is usually thin, so a visibly bulky isthmus should raise concern for diffuse goiter or gland enlargement.
neck-b51: Sialolithiasis means stones within a salivary duct or gland, most commonly the submandibular system. Memory tip: 'lith' means stone, so sialo-lithiasis literally means salivary stone disease.
neck-b52: The strap muscles are located anterior to the thyroid gland and include muscles such as the sternohyoid and sternothyroid. Remember: on ultrasound they appear as a thin hypoechoic layer overlying the thyroid.
neck-b53: The superior thyroid artery is the first branch of the external carotid artery. Key fact: it descends toward the upper pole of the thyroid, making it an important vascular landmark around thyroid nodules.
neck-b54: Psammoma bodies are tiny punctate calcific deposits, classically associated with papillary thyroid carcinoma. Remember: microcalcifications without shadowing in a thyroid nodule are a suspicious sonographic feature.
neck-b55: Iodine is not a thyroid hormone; it is an essential element used to synthesize thyroxine and triiodothyronine. Memory tip: the thyroid makes T4, T3, and calcitonin—not iodine itself.
neck-b56: Thyroxine (T4) is the most abundantly produced thyroid hormone. Remember: the thyroid secretes mostly T4, while the more active T3 is produced in smaller amounts and often converted peripherally from T4.
neck-b57: Sjögren syndrome is an autoimmune disorder that damages moisture-producing glands, causing dry eyes and dry mouth. Key memory fact: it commonly involves the salivary glands and can make them enlarged and heterogeneous on imaging.
neck-b58: The thyroid is an endocrine gland because it secretes hormones directly into the bloodstream. Remember: endocrine glands are ductless, unlike exocrine glands, which release products through ducts.
neck-b59: The pyramidal lobe is a superior extension of the thyroid isthmus and represents a remnant of embryologic thyroid descent. Memory tip: think of it as a small upward projection from the isthmus.
neck-b60: Mucoepidermoid carcinoma is the most common malignant salivary gland tumor, especially in the parotid gland. Remember: among salivary cancers, mucoepidermoid is the one most often tested as the most common.
male-b31: Primary varicoceles are usually left-sided, may cause infertility, and feel like a palpable extratesticular “bag of worms.” A retroperitoneal mass suggests a secondary varicocele, especially if new right-sided or nonreducible.
male-b32: A spermatocele is the classic cystic lesion in the epididymal head that contains nonviable sperm. Remember: epididymal head cyst + sperm content = spermatocele.
male-b33: Varicocele results from incompetent valves in the pampiniform plexus, causing dilated scrotal veins. Key memory aid: pampiniform plexus failure produces the palpable “bag of worms.”
male-b34: Alpha-fetoprotein is a recognized tumor marker used in evaluating testicular malignancy, especially nonseminomatous germ cell tumors. Remember AFP rises with yolk sac elements and is not produced by pure seminoma.
male-b35: The blue-dot sign classically indicates torsion of a testicular appendage, where the ischemic appendage is seen through the scrotal skin. Key fact: testicular blood flow is usually preserved.
male-b36: Varicocele is strongly associated with male infertility because venous congestion can impair spermatogenesis. High-yield fact: it is the most common correctable cause of male infertility.
male-b37: The corpus spongiosum surrounds and houses the male urethra along the ventral penis. Memory tip: the spongiosum “supports the stream.”
male-b38: In torsion of the testicular appendage, intratesticular flow is typically preserved, so absent testicular flow points instead to spermatic cord torsion. Common associated findings include a reactive hydrocele and scrotal wall thickening.
male-b39: Varicocele is the most common correctable cause of male infertility. Remember the classic association: left-sided “bag of worms” varicocele and abnormal semen parameters.
male-b40: A hydrocele is a simple fluid collection surrounding the testis. Key fact: it most commonly lies between the two layers of the tunica vaginalis.
male-b41: Squamous cell carcinoma is the most common malignancy of the penis. Remember: penile cancer is classically SCC, often arising from the epithelium.
male-b42: Peyronie disease causes painful penile curvature and erectile dysfunction due to fibrous plaque formation in the tunica albuginea. Memory tip: Peyronie = plaque leads to pain and bending.
male-b43: The testicles’ exocrine function is sperm production within the seminiferous tubules. Key contrast: testosterone production is the endocrine function of Leydig cells.
male-b44: A hydrocele most commonly collects between the visceral and parietal layers of the tunica vaginalis. Remember: it surrounds the testis but is outside the tunica albuginea.
male-b45: Testicular torsion classically presents with sudden acute testicular pain, often occurring at rest. Key fact: it is a surgical emergency because prolonged ischemia threatens testicular viability.
male-b1: Pyocele is an infected complex fluid collection in the tunica vaginalis, often developing as a complication of epididymo-orchitis with fever. Remember: hydrocele is usually simple anechoic fluid, whereas pyocele contains debris, septations, and inflammatory features.
male-b2: Testicular torsion typically causes acute pain, nausea, and swelling, and the affected testis is often high-riding with a horizontal lie. Remember: a lower, vertically oriented painful testis is least consistent with torsion.
male-b3: Intravaginal torsion is also called spermatic cord torsion and is linked to bell-clapper deformity and sometimes strenuous activity. Remember: torsion is most common in adolescents, not typically in the third or fourth decade.
male-b4: An elevated AFP strongly points to a yolk sac tumor, the most common testicular tumor in young children and a malignant germ cell tumor. Remember: seminomas do not produce AFP, so AFP elevation is a key clue away from seminoma.
male-b5: The classic serum tumor markers for testicular cancer are AFP, hCG, and LDH. Remember: FSH is a pituitary reproductive hormone, not a standard tumor marker for testicular malignancy.
male-b6: Buck fascia is the deep fascial covering that surrounds the corpora cavernosa and corpus spongiosum of the penis. Remember: Buck fascia encloses the erectile bodies, while tunica albuginea directly covers each erectile tissue structure.
male-b7: The tunica albuginea is the dense fibrous capsule tightly adherent to the testicle. Remember: it also extends inward to form septa, dividing the testis into lobules.
male-b8: The epididymis is divided into the head, body, and tail. Remember: there is no epididymal 'neck' division in standard anatomy.
male-b9: The Cowper glands are the bulbourethral glands, located inferior to the prostate and contributing lubricating secretions. Remember: 'Cowper = bulbourethral' is a classic anatomy synonym.
male-b10: The pampiniform plexus provides venous drainage of the testicles and helps cool arterial blood for temperature regulation. Remember: dilation of this plexus produces a varicocele.
male-b11: Teratomas contain tissues from multiple germ layers, so cartilage, bone, and fibrous tissue are classic components. Remember: their mixed tissue content often creates a heterogeneous testicular mass with calcifications.
male-b12: Prostatitis commonly causes painful ejaculation and may be associated with hematospermia due to inflammation of the prostate. Remember: infection/inflammation of the prostate often presents with pelvic pain plus urinary or ejaculatory symptoms.
male-b13: Klinefelter syndrome is classically associated with infertility, gynecomastia, and tall stature with long legs, but cryptorchidism is not a typical feature. Remember: think 47,XXY with small firm testes and hypogonadism.
male-b14: After vasectomy, the epididymis may enlarge from sperm stasis and back-pressure changes. Remember: post-vasectomy sonography often shows epididymal prominence rather than testicular atrophy or reduced testicular perfusion.
male-b15: An intratesticular varicocele appears as serpiginous tubular venous channels within the testis, often showing venous flow and augmentation with Valsalva. Remember: varicoceles are venous dilations, so Doppler confirmation is key.
male-b16: PSA is prostate-specific antigen, a protein made by prostatic tissue and commonly measured when evaluating BPH or prostate cancer. Remember: PSA is prostate-specific, but not cancer-specific, because it can rise in benign enlargement too.
male-b17: Sertoli cell tumors occur in younger patients and can produce estrogens, leading to gynecomastia. Key memory fact: estrogen-producing testicular tumors often present with feminizing features such as breast enlargement.
male-b18: Torsion of the appendix testis is classically associated with a small avascular extratesticular appendage and focal superior pole pain. Remember the 'blue dot sign' is a classic clinical clue for torsion of a testicular appendage.
