male-b19: Multiple tiny nonshadowing echogenic foci in both testes describe testicular microlithiasis, which has been associated with infertility. Key fact: microlithiasis appears as numerous punctate echoes without posterior shadowing.
male-b20: Chlamydia is a common infectious cause of epididymitis, especially in younger sexually active males. Remember: epididymitis often starts in the epididymal tail and shows increased blood flow on Doppler.
male-b21: The epididymis is attached to the posterior testis and is not part of the spermatic cord. A key memory aid is that the spermatic cord contains vessels, nerves, and the vas deferens as it courses through the inguinal canal.
male-b22: Seminoma is the most common malignant testicular tumor overall. Key fact: seminomas often appear as a homogeneous hypoechoic intratesticular mass and typically occur in men 30 to 50 years old.
male-b23: A left-sided varicocele is usually primary because the left testicular vein drains into the left renal vein, making left-sided varicoceles common. Secondary varicoceles are more concerning when right-sided or associated with a renal/abdominal mass.
male-b24: BPH most commonly arises in the transitional zone of the prostate, surrounding the proximal urethra. Remember: transitional zone enlargement explains the urinary obstruction symptoms seen with BPH.
male-b25: Multiple small cystic spaces along the mediastinum testis are typical of tubular ectasia of the rete testis. Key fact: this benign condition often occurs in older men and may coexist with epididymal obstruction or spermatoceles.
male-b26: In older men, prostate enlargement is most commonly due to benign prostatic hyperplasia. Remember: BPH is a benign nodular enlargement, usually centered in the transitional zone.
male-b27: An epidermoid cyst is a benign intratesticular lesion with a classic whorled or onion-skin appearance from concentric layers of keratin. Key fact: it usually lacks internal vascularity on Doppler.
male-b28: A spermatocele is a cystic lesion in the epididymal head that may contain low-level echoes or debris. Remember: spermatoceles are extratesticular, which helps distinguish them from intratesticular cystic lesions.
male-b29: A varicocele is a dilated collection of veins within the scrotum, usually in the pampiniform plexus. Key fact: it often enlarges with Valsalva and is more common on the left side.
male-b30: Adrenal rest tissue can mimic a solid intratesticular mass and is associated with endocrine disorders such as Cushing syndrome. Remember: adrenal rests are linked to excess adrenal stimulation and can be bilateral.
male-b46: Torsion of the testicular appendage classically causes focal pain at the superior pole in boys and may produce the blue-dot sign. Remember: appendage torsion is usually localized superiorly, whereas true testicular torsion more often involves the entire testis.
male-b47: Zinner syndrome is the male counterpart of Mayer-Rokitansky-type anomalies and includes unilateral renal agenesis, ejaculatory duct obstruction, and ipsilateral seminal vesicle cysts. Remember the triad: kidney absent, duct blocked, seminal vesicle cystic.
male-b48: A varicocele is diagnosed when pampiniform plexus veins measure greater than 2 mm, especially if they enlarge with Valsalva. Remember: '2 mm or more' is the classic sonographic threshold.
male-b49: Bell-clapper deformity means the testis lacks normal posterior fixation, allowing it to swing freely and predisposing to torsion. Remember: a freely mobile testis is a torsion risk factor.
male-b50: The Valsalva maneuver increases intra-abdominal pressure and accentuates venous reflux, making a varicocele more evident on ultrasound. Remember: varicoceles often enlarge and show more flow with Valsalva.
male-b51: The testes' endocrine role is testosterone production by Leydig cells, while sperm production is the exocrine function. Remember: Leydig = testosterone; seminiferous tubules = sperm.
male-b52: Hyperemic intratesticular flow is not typical of testicular torsion; torsion usually shows decreased or absent flow compared with the normal side. Remember: torsion cuts off blood supply, not increases it.
male-b53: Spermatogenesis occurs in the seminiferous tubules within the testicular parenchyma. Remember: seminiferous tubules make sperm, while the rete testis helps collect and transport it.
male-b54: Cryptorchidism means one or both testes failed to descend into the scrotum. Remember: undescended testes are often located in the inguinal canal and carry increased infertility and malignancy risk.
male-b55: Seminoma is the most common germ cell tumor of the testis and often appears as a homogeneous hypoechoic mass. Remember: seminoma is the classic most common adult testicular tumor.
male-b56: Varicoceles are most common on the left because the left testicular vein drains into the left renal vein, increasing venous pressure. Remember: left-sided varicocele is the classic presentation.
male-b57: Most prostate cancers arise in the peripheral zone, which is why many are palpable on digital rectal exam. Remember: peripheral zone is the common cancer zone; BPH usually affects the transitional zone.
male-b58: A testicular abscess typically shows no internal flow because the center is liquefied, with hyperemia in the surrounding inflamed tissue. Remember: abscess = avascular center, hyperemic rim.
male-b59: Prostate cancer is the most common cancer diagnosed in men. Remember: although lung cancer causes many cancer deaths, prostate cancer is the most commonly found male malignancy.
male-b60: A seminoma most commonly appears as a well-defined hypoechoic intratesticular mass on sonography. Remember: seminomas are usually more homogeneous than nonseminomatous germ cell tumors.
msk-b1: Staphylococcus is a common bacterial cause of cellulitis, producing skin and soft-tissue infection with redness, warmth, and swelling. Remember: cellulitis is usually bacterial, and Staph and Strep are the classic organisms.
msk-b2: An abscess typically shows peripheral hyperemia on color Doppler because inflamed tissue around the fluid collection has increased blood flow. Memory tip: pus in the center is often avascular, but the rim is “hot” and hyperemic.
msk-b3: A Baker cyst is also called a popliteal cyst because it occurs in the popliteal fossa behind the knee. Remember: Baker = back of the knee.
msk-b4: Meniscal cysts are commonly associated with prior trauma or an underlying meniscal tear. Key fact: a history of knee injury helps distinguish a meniscal cyst from other soft-tissue masses.
msk-b5: Sonography is especially useful for radiolucent foreign bodies because they may not be visible on x-ray. Remember: wood, plastic, and some organic materials are radiolucent but often conspicuous on ultrasound.
msk-b6: Arthrogryposis is a congenital disorder characterized by severe joint contractures present at birth. Memory tip: “arthro” refers to joints and “gryposis” suggests curvature or stiffness.
msk-b7: In a lactating patient with focal erythema, swelling, fever, and pain, a breast abscess is the most likely diagnosis. Key fact: infection during breastfeeding can progress from mastitis to a drainable abscess.
msk-b8: A white blood cell count is often elevated with a breast abscess because it reflects active infection and inflammation. Remember: WBCs rise when the body is fighting bacteria.
msk-b9: A seroma commonly develops after surgical removal of a breast lesion as a postoperative fluid collection. Key fact: seromas are typically simple fluid pockets in the surgical bed.
msk-b10: Subluxation is identified when the hip appears stable without stress but partially displaces with stress. Remember: subluxation means partial, not complete, displacement of the femoral head.
msk-b11: A ganglion cyst is a common painless cystic mass of the wrist arising near a joint capsule or tendon sheath. Memory tip: the wrist is the classic location for a ganglion.
msk-b12: If a wrist abnormality is located near the radial artery on the palmar aspect, it is termed volar. Remember: volar refers to the anterior/palm side of the wrist and hand.
msk-b13: The meniscus is a thin fibrocartilaginous structure within the knee that is prone to tearing. Key fact: the medial and lateral menisci act as shock absorbers between the femur and tibia.
msk-b14: Estrogen is the maternal hormone associated with ligamentous laxity and is thought to contribute to developmental dysplasia of the hip. Remember: increased laxity can make the neonatal hip less stable.
msk-b15: The gastrocnemius is the major calf muscle forming much of the posterior lower leg contour. Memory tip: the calf is largely gastrocnemius above and soleus deeper below.
msk-b16: The deltoid is the large lateral shoulder muscle and a common site for intramuscular injections, so a painful post-injection mass there would be in the deltoid. Remember: deltoid = the "shoulder cap" muscle.
msk-b17: Radial and antiradial scanning follows the natural ductal anatomy of the breast, making duct patterns easier to trace and evaluate. Remember: breast ducts radiate toward the nipple like spokes on a wheel.
msk-b18: The wrist bones are called the carpals. A quick memory aid: carpals = carpus = wrist, while metacarpals are the hand bones farther distal.
msk-b19: Renal adenocarcinoma is not a typical cause of gynecomastia, whereas endocrine disorders, marijuana use, and some tumors can be associated with male breast enlargement. Remember: gynecomastia usually relates to hormone imbalance.
msk-b20: The Thompson test assesses Achilles tendon rupture, so it is least helpful for a hemorrhagic mass behind the knee, such as a popliteal cyst complication. Remember: posterior knee mass workup focuses on Doppler flow and joint communication.
msk-b21: The Graf technique is the ultrasound method that measures alpha and beta angles to assess the relationship between the femoral head and acetabulum. Remember: Graf = hip dysplasia angles.
msk-b22: Cellulitis is infection and inflammation involving the skin and subcutaneous tissues. Remember: on ultrasound, cellulitis often shows a "cobblestone" appearance in the soft tissues.
msk-b23: Pain, edema, and warmth are common signs of tendonitis, but itching is not a typical clinical feature. Remember: tendonitis is an inflammatory process, so think pain and heat rather than pruritus.
msk-b24: The Ortolani test evaluates whether a dislocated infant hip can be reduced or relocated back into the acetabulum. Remember: Ortolani = "out and in" reduction maneuver.
msk-b25: The Thompson test helps diagnose an Achilles tendon tear by squeezing the calf and observing for plantar flexion. Remember: absent foot movement with calf squeeze suggests Achilles rupture.
msk-b26: A cystic mass in the popliteal fossa is most commonly a Baker cyst, which arises from the posterior knee joint region. Remember: Baker cyst = classic cyst behind the knee.
msk-b27: A pilonidal cyst commonly occurs in the natal cleft and may present as a painful, draining or oozing mass. Remember: pilonidal disease is classically located near the sacrococcygeal cleft.
msk-b28: A ganglion cyst is the most common mass along the dorsal hand and wrist. Remember: dorsal wrist lump in an adult is ganglion until proven otherwise.
msk-b29: The Achilles tendon attaches the calf muscles to the heel bone, so it connects the heel to the calf muscle. Remember: gastrocnemius and soleus join to form the Achilles tendon.
msk-b30: The prone position best exposes the posterior ankle and heel, allowing optimal sonographic evaluation of the Achilles tendon. Remember: Achilles imaging is easiest from behind, so place the patient prone.
msk-b31: Puerperal mastitis is breast inflammation associated with pregnancy and lactation, typically occurring postpartum during breastfeeding. Remember: "puerperal" refers to the period shortly after childbirth.
msk-b32: The Thompson test is performed with the patient prone while the examiner squeezes the calf to observe for plantarflexion. Key memory aid: absent plantarflexion suggests Achilles tendon rupture.
msk-b33: Lipomas are usually soft, mobile, benign fatty masses that are typically painless. Remember: pain is unusual with a simple lipoma and may suggest another process or complication.
msk-b34: Subluxation means a partial dislocation of a joint, commonly discussed at the hip when alignment is incomplete but not fully lost. Remember: subluxation is less severe than a complete dislocation.
msk-b35: This is the exception because most foreign bodies are not hypoechoic; they are usually echogenic and may cast shadowing or show comet-tail artifact. Remember: wood, glass, and metal often stand out as bright reflectors.
msk-b36: A hypoechoic fluid collection elevating the hip joint capsule in a child is classic for joint effusion. Remember: pediatric hip effusion often presents with limp, irritability, and low-grade fever.
msk-b37: A lipoma is a benign tumor made of adipose tissue. Remember: "lipo-" means fat, making lipoma the classic benign fatty mass.
msk-b38: Transient synovitis is the most common cause of hip joint effusion in infants and young children. Remember: it often follows a recent viral illness and is usually self-limited.
msk-b39: A hemangioma is a benign tumor composed of blood vessels. Remember: "hema-" refers to blood, which helps link hemangioma to vascular tissue.
msk-b40: A high-frequency linear array transducer provides the best resolution for superficial structures like a splinter in the hand. Remember: high frequency for superficial detail, linear for near-field imaging.
msk-b41: A Baker cyst forms when synovial fluid distends the popliteal bursa from knee joint capsule weakness, often with rheumatoid arthritis. Remember: Baker cysts are classically found in the popliteal fossa behind the knee.
msk-b42: Fluid within the synovial sheath indicates inflammation of the tendon sheath, which is tendosynovitis. Remember: tendon plus synovial sheath involvement distinguishes it from isolated tendonitis.
msk-b43: Gynecomastia most commonly appears as a hypoechoic retroareolar mass-like region on ultrasound. Remember: its central subareolar location helps distinguish it from many male breast malignancies.
msk-b44: Refractive shadowing occurs when the sound beam bends at the edge of a curved structure, producing an edge shadow. Remember: this artifact is commonly seen at the margins of cysts and rounded structures.
msk-b45: Tendosynovitis is inflammation involving both the tendon and its synovial sheath. Remember: the "synov" portion tells you the sheath is involved, not just the tendon alone.
msk-b46: A localized complex fluid collection in an area of cellulitis with fever, edema, and focal tenderness is most consistent with a superficial abscess. Remember: cellulitis is diffuse soft-tissue infection, while an abscess is a walled-off fluid collection.
msk-b47: A thin flap of tissue within a complicated Baker cyst is called pannus. Memory tip: pannus refers to inflamed synovial tissue that can extend into cystic collections around joints.
msk-b48: A Bible bump is the common name for a ganglion cyst, usually found near the wrist or hand. Remember: ganglion cysts are classic fluid-filled masses arising from a joint capsule or tendon sheath.
msk-b49: A Baker cyst can clinically mimic deep venous thrombosis because both may cause calf pain and swelling. Key fact: a ruptured Baker cyst especially can resemble DVT, so ultrasound helps distinguish them.
msk-b50: Normal muscle is typically hypoechoic with linear echogenic fibroadipose strands running through it. Think: muscle looks dark overall, with bright striations creating its characteristic pennate appearance.
msk-b51: This statement is false because ganglion cysts are common around the hand and wrist, not between the tarsals as described. Remember: they most often arise on the dorsal wrist near a joint or tendon sheath.
msk-b52: A partial tendon tear usually appears as a focal hypoechoic defect within the tendon fibers. Key fact: complete tears more often show full discontinuity with possible retraction, while partial tears are localized.
msk-b53: Tendons are echogenic, fibrous structures that connect muscle to bone. Memory aid: ligaments connect bone to bone, whereas tendons transmit muscle force to bone.
msk-b54: A standoff pad improves visualization of superficial structures by bringing them into the focal zone. Remember: it adds near-field distance, which helps evaluate very shallow lesions more clearly.
msk-b55: Hyperemic flow in or around a structure usually indicates inflammation because inflamed tissue has increased vascularity. Key fact: color or power Doppler is useful for detecting this increased blood flow.
msk-b56: Scanning the patient standing with pressure on the symptomatic side is not part of standard Achilles tendon assessment. Remember: optimal evaluation is usually done prone, comparing both sides in long- and short-axis planes.
msk-b57: The Thompson test is performed by squeezing the calf; the foot should plantarflex if the Achilles tendon is intact. Key fact: absent plantarflexion suggests a complete Achilles tendon tear.
msk-b58: Lipomas may be hypo-, iso-, or hyperechoic relative to surrounding tissue, but they are not typically anechoic. Remember: anechoic usually suggests simple fluid, whereas lipomas are solid fatty masses.
msk-b59: Metallic foreign bodies such as bullets or shrapnel commonly produce comet-tail artifact because of reverberation from the highly reflective surface. Memory tip: bright metal often creates repeated echoes trailing deep to the object.
msk-b60: Air around a foreign body produces bright echogenic reflections that can obscure or confuse the true orientation of the object. Remember: even tiny amounts of gas are highly reflective on ultrasound.
